REMUNERATION OF RURAL DELIVERY MAIL CARRIERS.
speechtext:
1.	Has the attention of the Government been drawn to the state of dissatisfaction existing among the rural delivery mail carriers because of the inadequate scale of remuneration consequent upon the increased cost of living?
2.	If so, is it the intention of the Government to modify existing contracts and to increase the rate of pay to the rural carriers in future contracts so as to provide for relief as justified by said increased cost of living and the increased cost of rural delivery?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REMUNERATION OF RURAL DELIVERY MAIL CARRIERS.
speechtext:
1 and 2. A number of appeals have been received from rural mail contractors for increased remuneration on account of the increased cost of living. Each appeal is considered on its own merits, due regard being paid to the present rate of remuneration and the date on which the contract was entered into.
The policy of the Government is to do everything possible to ameliorate the financial conditions of the rural mail couriers, but the Post Office Act makes it unlawful to increase the rate paid to a mail contractor without first inviting public tenders except when an addition is made to the regular service or when it can be shown that the quantity of mail matter which he is required to convey has increased to such an extent as to necessitate the employment of additional equipment and couriers.
If investigation shows that a contractor entered into his contract at a time so recent as to make it possible to foresee and consequently provide against the increase in operating expenses, there could be no good grounds for any drastic action by the Government to release him; but if on The other hand, the contractor entered into his obligations at a time when it was impossible to foresee the sudden rise in the cost of operation, and is consequently, through no fault of his own, carrying on his work at

a loss, steps are taken to invite tenders with a view to making other satisfactory contract arrangements which when completed would lead to his release.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in the interests of the public service of this country and in justice to a discharged official, the Public Utilities Commissioner of Manitoba be authorized to investigate the summary dismissal, in the autumn of 1917, of James Conner, who for many years served the country as a preventive officer, and that he report his findings to this House, coupled with a recommendation as' to what action should be taken in order that justice shall be achieved.
He said: Before the motion is put, Mr. Speaker, I desire to speak briefly to it. This is the third occasion on which I have made an attempt to secure justice for a faithful official. I have already told the story to the House at two previous sessions and I purpose to tell jt again. I want to ascertain for myself whether or not justice can be obtained for an official who served this country as faithfully as he knew how for

twenty long years, and who was summarily dismissed, receiving notice, I think, on October 4 that his services were dispensed with as from the 30th of the previous month. I brought the matter to the attention of the House two sessions ago and was promised by the Minister of Immigration that it would be investigated and that justice would be done-I think he said that justice would be done. Nothing, however, was done in the case, and last session I again brought the matter to the attention of the House when the present Acting. Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) gave his pledge that there would be a thorough investigation to the end that justice might be meted out to this official. Up to the present time, so far as I know, absolutely nothing has been done. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to cross the floor of the House and take a place with the Opposition, nor do I wish to ally myself at present with the party led by my hon. friend the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), but I do want to ascertain whether or not justice can be done by this Union Government which I have stood by with more or less faithfulness since its constitution. Of course, if justice cannot be obtained from the Government it may be necessary for me to organize a party of my/ own, and I will see that the right thing is done.
A one-man party.
Well, never mind. Some great movements have been started by eminent men, though perhaps they were not so great as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau).

May I ask my hon. friend
if he expects participating in the salary of the leader of the Opposition in the event of his crossing the floor of the House?

No. I am quite free to say to my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Peck) that if ever I attained to the position of leader of the Opposition I should not ask for nor expect any salary. I should take the position free, gratis and for nothing, and discharge its duties to the very best of my ability. But, joking aside, Mr. Speaker, I desire to present, as briefly as I possibly can, the facts of this case.
Twenty years ago, when the boundary was largely unguarded, I succeeded in inducing the Government to appoint a Scotchman named James Conner, who lived along the boundary, to protect the wood that existed in such abundance to the north.
I think he received a salary of $200 a year, but he guarded that boundary with ex-

emplary faithfulness. Later on, when it was necessary to have a preventive officer in that locality, Mr. Conner was appointed to the position, and I think he was given a salary of $600 a year. It is a long time since I represented that constituency, but Mr. Conner continued in that position as preventive officer with the 

 salary I have mentioned. At a later stage I shall state what his collections were in order that hon. members may form some idea of his efficiency. When the immigration from the United States began to pour into that part of the country, Mr. Conner was appointed Immigration Officer with an additional salary of $100, and in that connection for twelve years he guarded the boundary. He looked after all the immigrants for twelve years, during which time immigration poured into the country. Now, a little over two years ago when immigration ceased and coincident with the time the Union Government was organized, a petty conspiracy on the part of some understrappers was hatched against Mr. Conner, and he was notified that his services would be no longer required. As I have already said, he received notice on the 4th of October, his dismissal taking effect in September. I wish hon. members would listen carefully to this statement, because I am sure their hearts would burn with the same indignation that filled mine when the facts were presented to me. Mr. Conner knew me and wrote to me telling me of the facts, and I wrote to the late John MacDougald, Commissioner of Customs, who informed me that the man was dismissed on the ground of economy, and that a man named Nesbitt had been sent from Winnipeg to take his place. I instituted inquiries and ascertained that Nesbitt had been appointed Preventive Officer under the Customs Department at a salary, I think, of $1,050 for one office alone, whereas this man had rendered admirable service for twenty years, the last twelve years of which period he had done work for the Immigration Department for an additional $100. Yet he was dismissed on the ground of economy, forsooth! I naturally was indignant over the whole matter, and after being elected I made an investigation that convinced me that there had been great injustice to an official whose service's had been absolutely beyond reproach. I therefore brought the matter to the attention of the House, for I know not of any other way to obtain justice for this man. I am not engaged in wire-pulling with any minister or the officers of any department. As a member of the House I like to present

the facts of any case such as this right on the floor of Parliament, because I am satisfied that the sense of justice which must be alive in the mind of every hon. member must recognize that justice is imperative in this instance. The man has done faithful iwork for twenty years, and I am determined to urge his case, and to lay the circumstances before the House as forcefully as I possibly can, until justice is obtained.
When I found out what the facts were, as I have already said, I immediately brought the matter to the attention of the House and I received a pledge from the right hon. gentleman who is acting as Prime Minister. I may read from Hansard what took place in the House. In the course of my remarks I said:

I felt I would keep at this thing to And out whether justice could be obtained in a case of this kind. If the position had been given to a returned soldier, probably Mr. Conner would have been perfectly satisfied and so would I.

I will try my very best to give a declaration after what the hon. gentleman has been good enough to say about me. I do not know the least thing about the case except that I have heard the story of my hon. friend. I am not impugning that at ail; it is, I dare say, correct, but I think I will have to ask my hon. friend to await an answer from the responsible head of the department- it is very dangerous work mixing in with the business of colleagues
If the right hon. leader of the House will say that when the papers come down, if he is leading the House at the end of the session, he will make a declaration, I will subside at once.

I can do that right away. A declaration will be made either by the responsible minister or by myself.
The papers came down, and what did they show? Did they show that this man was inefficient? No; they showed that one of these men .in the conspiracy that was formed to injure Conner wrote to Thomas Geliy. Immigration Agent in Winnipeg, to endeavour if possible to fish up some information that this man was not efficient. Finally Mr. Geliy was compelled to report that Mr. Conner was entirely efficient. I looked over the reports, and found that the immigration inspector 'had .reported the man ais being highly capable, and I may inform the House that it would be impossible, if you went over the province of Manitoba with a fine-toothed comb, to discover a more thoroughly reliable man, a man of more unquestionable integrity and sterling worth than Mr. Conner. For the last thirty or forty years he has lived on the plains in Manitoba, having raised a large' family of some ten children. With 27
that family he has farmed some eight or ten sections of land, and in the early days, I may say, he used to be an engineer, running a threshing machine at three or foui-o'clock in the .morning with the thermometer down to twenty-five and thirty below zero, in an effort to earn sufficient money to keep the roof over his family. I think, therefore, in view of all the circumstances, it is a matter of grave injustice that a man of strict sobriety and integrity Should be .summarily dismissed for inefficiency, when his career distinctly shows absolutely the reverse. It was not a matter of inefficiency, by any means, Mr. Speaker, there was a conspiracy hatched by understrappers in the department, and as a result of their machinations this man was dismissed from a post he bad filled so well for such a long time. As I say, my indignation naturally burned over the affair, and I was impelled to bring the matter to the attention of .this House on two previous occasions, and aim bringing it again. No action having been taken by the responsible department, I am now asking that the Public Utilities Commissioner of Manitoba, a man of great probity, Mr. P. A. McDonald, who enjoys the implicit confidence of the community, be .asked to make an investigation. It is due this faithful public servant that he be vindicated. He lies under the stigma of having been dismissed for lack of efficiency, and he should he vindicated without undue delay. He drew only a small salary and was a comparatively obscure official, but that - is no reason why justice should not he done him by Parliament. In our eyes he ought to have the same protection as if he occupied the highest "position in the land. Let us do him justice, Mr. Speaker; let us ascertain whether he was really inefficient. I simply ask that the Utilities Commissioner of Manitoba make an investigation into the matter. I think it is due to Mr. Conner that this step should be taken and that this House Should know whether or not he has been improperly treated. I further ask that a recommendation be made as to what should be done in the premises. Mr. Conner said to me: "I am not asking that you shall give me my job back if there is a returned soldier who desires it, but I do ask to be vindicated." And that is what I demand this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. I am satisfied that no hon. member who has listened to the facts as I have recounted them will decline to support this motion. All I ask is that justice-simple common justice-be done to as faithful a public



servant as ever occupied a position in the public service of this country. I deeply regret that my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Bolton) is not here. He knows all about the facts. He promised me that he would second the motion, present the facts to the House and endorse what I have said.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry that the hon. member for Lisgar is not here because I understood the hon. member for Springfield to point in his direction and I named him as the seconder of the motion. Not being in the House, he, of course, cannot second the motion.
I am sure there is some man in the House who will second the motion.
I will second the motion.
Certainly; I am sure the leader of the Opposition or any other member would second the motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is purely a question of observing the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I am not familiar with the matter that my hon. friend has taken up but as I have only recently taken charge of the Department of Customs-

I beg your pardon but I would like to make a few remarks with reference to this matter before the Minister speaks. The hon.. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) opened his lemarks by saying that this matter had been brought before the House for the third time. I am aware of it because this is the third tame that I have heard him speak about this man Conner. I am not interested in the matter except for the sake of seeing that justice is done. Upon the declaration made by the hon. member for Springfield, it appears to me that he has established a prima facie case. I cannot understand a member of Parliament and a supporter of the Government -standing up on the floor of this House and saying to the Government that he 'is here for the third time bringing up a matter, which at first sight, and on presentation of the case, shows a gross injustice done to this man James Conner. My hon. friend is now here for (he third time asking his own party to do justice in a case where injustice is absolutely apparent. But the hon. member for Springfield goes further. He says that he is going to bring this matter up year after year until justice has been done to James
[Mr. Richardson.!
Conner. I do not blame him for doing it, not because he is speaking against his own party but because I think that a member of Parliament who brings up a question like this o>ves it to himself, to his own responsibility and to his own dignity to see that justice is done. Consequently I would ask the Government to act in such a way that this question shall not again he brought before Parliament. This case with reference to James Conner is going to cost the country quite a lot of money if my hon. friend from Springfield who, I hope, may be a member of this House for many years, is going to bring it before Parliament year after year and rve are going to sit here year after year listening to his appeals to his own party without his being able to receive any satisfactory answer from them. These are the only remarks I have to make and I hope the Government will see fit to give a satisfactory answer to my hon. friend and do justice to this man, James -Conner, because if the facts as represented by the hon. member for Springfield are true-and no one has said so far that they are not true-there certainly has been' gross injustice done to this man and it is up to us to know whether we are going to see that this injustice -shall be remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have very little to say on this matter. As I remarked just now to my hon. friend from Springfield, being somewhat new in the Department of Customs, I am not familiar with the subject except in so far as he has brought it before the House. I saw the return when it was brought down. My recollection of it is that it was a statement by the Deputy Minister of the Interior referring to the inefficiency of Mr. Conner. I think it is quite obvious that it would be rather unusual for this House to appoint the Public Utilities Commissioner of Manitoba to investigate this particular case but I see no reason, in view of the impression that this man has suffered an injustice, why there should not be some additional investigation to ascertain whether or not an injustice has been done. As far as I am personally concerned I am quite willing that that course should be taken. It is possible that the Civil Service Commission might look into it, or, if not it might be taken up by our own Department. I appreciate what the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) has said that it is not desirable that, the time of this House should be taken up with matters of this kind being brought up again and again and I appreciate the

position of my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) who believes that there has been a real injustice done and he would like to have it remedied. I shall be only too glad to expedite inquiry in any reasonable way.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I would like
to add just ia word to what has been said by the Minister of Customs. It would appear that the Conner matter arose about the 5th October, 1917, and neither the present Minister of Customs nor I had anything to do with the incident.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Now as to the facts, because, after all, it is the facts that the House would like to have. I have discussed this matter on several occasions with the member for Springfield. It would appear that this man Conner had been in the public service for quite a while. He was in receipt of <a salary of some five or six hundred dollars from the Customs Department, and in addition about $100 from the Immigration Department. The member for Springfield knows Mr. Conner, I understand, well-has known him for years, knows him as a very respectable, law-abiding, decent citizen of the very best type.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Now on the other hand- whether it is true or not I do not know- the records of the department would indicate that in so far as Mr. Conner's services in the Immigration Department were concerned they were not looked on as satisfactory. I think the member for Springfield wall bear me out when I say that the files of the department indicate that-not for a short period, but a period extending over a considerable number of years
No, I entirely dissent from that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Well, that is a fact that will have to be ascertained.

The papers will
show.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I know that considerable stress is laid in the papers upon the file that Air. Conner was responsible-and 1 think contrary to warning, if I remember rightly-for allowing in a band of gypsies, whose admission cost the country a very large sum of money. In addition to that, it was almost impossible for the department to get any return or statement from him at all, and this went on for a considerable 271
length of time. I am not stating my view of the situation, I am merely trying to indicate what the departmental records show.
On the other hand, the member for Springfield has stated that there was a conspiracy on the part of certain understrappers in the department. Well, I do not know who were in the conspiracy, or why such a conspiracy should exist. I know that when I first took the matter up in the department, Air. Cory, who was acting as deputy minister, and Mr. Scott, who has been Superintendent of Immigration for years, intimated that in their judgment Mr. Conner was not capable of carryiiig on the work that the Immigration Department expected would be carried on at that point. That is their view, whether right or wrong. However, it seems to me that in view of the position taken by the member for -Spring-field-and I do not blame him at all if he considers there has been a grave injustice done this man, and if he thinks that the facts and statements set forth in the departmental records are -not correct-there is only one thing to do and that is to get the facts. It seems to me that those facts should be ascertained, not by the Public Utilities Commissioner of the province of Manitoba, but by some officer of the Federal -Government who can be trusted to do that work. I do not wish to enter into any controversy at the present time over the facts-I am merely trying to intimate what the record is -so far as the file itself shows it, and what the opinions of the officials o-f the department are, whether right or wrong, with reference to this man's work.
Although the member for Springfield -has had the opportunity, as he had last year of looking over the whole departmental record, if he is not satisfied-if lie considers that further investigation should be held, then I say we should grant that investigation in order to get at -the facts.
Air. Speaker, might I have the privilege, with the unanimous consent of the House, of saying a word or two further.

You have the right to do
so, you are closing the Debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon.
member for Springfield is exercising his right to reply. If any other member wishes to speak on this matter he should speak now.

I merely wish to
state in reply to what the minister has said that this incident occurred before the Union

Government came into office. I was not seeking to cast any blame-of course the ministers know I was not-upon the Union Government, although the Union Government might fall just as well as any other government. I wish to make this further statement.. I looked over the papers when they were brought down, and I found this extract in a letter written by the Deputy Minister of the Interior. That is what convinced me that there was a conspiracy. I will read the extract:
I believe that your officer at that point-
Referring to Mr. Conner-
-is very old, and, from what I can gather very inefficient. The Commissioners, who have been investigating our Immigration Service recommend that the duties of the two departments be combined and that Mr. Nesbitt be placed in charge, the cost of the service to be apportioned between the two departments.
This is the matter about which I spoke to you over the telephone. Will you please let me have confirmation of this arrangement.
Why should the Deputy Minister of the Interior confer with the late John McDou-gald, Commissioner of Customs, over the telephone about the dismissal, the sidetracking, of this very decent man? Then there is the attempt to discredit him, and even the minister has fallen into the snare. The Minister of Immigration says Mr. Conner was inefficient and that he let some gypsies into the country. Now let us see about that. For twelve long years of the period that immigration poured into the Northwest from the United States, this man Conner looked after the interests of the public in connection with that department, he did it for $100 a year, and not a single complaint that I could notice was ever made against him-I will refer to the matter of the gypsies later on. So far as regards the complaint of not reporting to the Department Conner reported every month. The minister has probably taken *his cue from some member of the Civil Service who has told or tried to tell him, not the facts, but a garbled story about the situation.
Now with regard to the gypsies, and that is a matter in regard to which the officials ring the changes against this old official, Mr. Conner. There were a number of gypsies who came to the province of Manitoba some years ago bringing with them $35,000. They should have made entry at Emmerson but they came to Mr. Conner who was the officer there. They had all *this money, they had their horses, and they had a lot of effects, and Mr. Conner naturally thought they were settlers and he

allowed them to go through. But when it was found that they had practised some deception-I think I am correct in my facts -at Emmerson the matter was reported to Winnipeg and these men were corailed, brought back and tried at the town of Morden. The minister says it cost the country a large sum of money but I do not think he knew what he was talking about. Just look at the position the Government was in at that time. The gypsies were brought up for trial at Morden. Do you suppose the Dominion Government offered any evidence against them? They did not even appear against these men at all, and they were dismissed and sent out of the country, and the cost was practically nothing-probably only a few cents or a few dollars to anybody. Then the officials start in to make it appear that Conner is an inefficient man. I think I have demonstrated to the satisfaction of this House that so far from Conner being inefficient he was the most efficient officer the department had in that country. Let me cite a few further facts, because it is worth while under the circumstances; I do not want this matter coming up every session, I want it settled right here and now. It is true the present Minister of Customs knows nothing about the matter; he has not held his present office during the last two sessions. But the Minister of Immigration and Colonization does know something about it and he might, I think- because I have great regard for him-and a personal liking-have seen that justice was done. He did not do that. The leader of the House (Sir George Foster) who enjoys the respect, I am sure, of every member of the House, gave his promise that justice should be done and I accepted that promise. I did so in good faith and I said " Now, at last, Mr. Conner will have a square deal," but I suppose in the multitude of his duties the Acting Prime Minister has neglected to see that Mr. Conner did get a square deal.
Now to show you to what extent this man Conner is neither inefficient nor useless let me read a few facts. At Bannerman, which is a little bit farther west than where he guards the boundary, the revenue in 1918 was $2,481, and the cost of collection was $2,317, very nearly the amount of the entire revenue. I do not wish to tire the House, but I would like the facts to be known. At Boissevain the revenue was $3,117, the cost $1,000; at Cartwright $604 and $900, so that the country lost $300; at Deloraine $2,145 and $900; at Killarney $1,260 and $900; at Crystal city $1,777 and $1,000; at

Morden $2,887 and $1,050; at Hasket $2,208 and the salaries $1,394. But at Snowflake, where this prime old servant James Conner looked after the revenue, the collections in 1918 were $4,622 or nearly double the amount collected by any other officer in that territory. At what cost to the country? He got only $650 as Customs Officer and $100 as Immigration Officer, so it cost only $650 to collect $4,622. Yet all the other men were let go scot free, while this faithful servant, who collected nearly double the amount of revenue collected by any of the others, was dismissed for inefficiency.

Have you got the
figures for last year?

No. I do not know what the collections would be, but I suppose they would be about the same, although the salary has been doubled. On the grounds of inefficiency and economy this fine old public servant was dismissed and a man appointed in his place at double the salary. It is such an outrageous proceeding that I marvel that my motion is not accepted at once. I am tired of bringing this matter before the department officials. I want a recommendation that will do justice to this faithful servant. Let us vindicate him. Let us not turn him adrift on the ground that he was inefficient and too old to serve his country. How will you ever get faithful service unless you treat your most menial official justly? You must give him fair play or you cannot expect decent service.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I have fully covered the ground. I do not at all like the suggestion that the matter should be left to the department, because it will simply be glossed over. Let us settle it now. Let us name some tribunal to investigate this case. I lay awake many hours thinking and I finally hit upon the Public Utilities Commissioner of Manitoba, a man of honour and probity, as the best gentleman to investigate and report on the matter. But if the Government knows " a better 'ole '[DOT] let them go to it. I will accept any decent investigator, but I do not want to sit down without having a decision as to what shall be done. Let us have an investigation to ascertain whether this decent old man has been justly or unjustly treated, so that I may not be forced to bother the House with this case session after session. If the Government will put their heads together and name any other reasonable tribunal it will be acceptable to me, but I want the matter settled now.

speechtext:
I would suggest to the hon.
member that the other ministers and myself see him and arrange for some official, satisfactory to him, to deal with this matter.
Somebody satisfactory to me?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

I will be perfectly
satisfied. That settles it then.

speakeroldname: Mr. CHARLES GAVAN POWER (Quebec South) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the ancient walls and fortifications of the city of Quebec, having for all military purposes become abso-lete, it is expedient in order to better preserve these valuable heirlooms as a historical monument for future generations, that their upkeep and control be now vested in the National Battlefields Commission.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject which I wish to bring up for discussion to-day has been on the Order Paper for quite a long time. It is a proposal that the walls and fortifications of the city of Quebec be now taken from the control of the Militia Department and placed in an independent commission. I am pleased indeed to see the Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Hugh Guthrie) in his seat, and before I go any further I wish to tell him that this scheme has had the approval of his predecessor and also of Sir Sam Hughes, former Minister of Militia.
The walls and fortifications have become absolutely obsolete and useless for warlike purposes. They could not withstand a five minute bombardment by modem artillery. They would be, I imagine, more a source of danger than defence to those who manned them.
Hitherto their control and upkeep has been vested in the Department of Militia and Defence. This department, very wisely I imagine, is not too wasteful of the public moneys, and does not wish to expend money for the defence of Canada where such expenditure would be useless. Therefore I propose to rid the department of what to-day must be very much of an incumbrance.
By 7-8 Edward VII, Chap. 57, there has been created a body called " The National Battlefields Commission." This commission

was constituted because, according to the preamble of the Statute:
It is desirable in the public interest of Canada to acquire and preserve the great historic battlefields at Quebec, restoring so far as possible their principal features,
To this Commission the Federal and Provincial Governments have at various times voted considerable sums, and societies and private individuals have generously contributed. I may say in passing that that Commission has performed splendid work in Quebec, as anybody who has been there recently may see. We have a splendid Battlefields Park on the Plains of Abraham, where formerly a wilderness existed.
Now, I propose, subject of course to any considerations of military necessity, that these fortifications be taken over by this Battlefields Commission. It is not my desire to hasten the (Government into adopting any scheme that may be impossible or impracticable, and I quite understand that there may be reasons of State to prevent their taking the action I suggest; for instance, the Imperial authorities in handing over the citadel and fortifications to the Canadian Government may have placed some restrictions upon their use, but of that I have no knowledge. I simply wish to ask that serious consideration be given to this subject, feeling assured that the public service will be benefited and its efficiency increased without putting one cent more cost on the public funds.
I have already stated that the value of these fortifications for practical purposes is useless. We must not forget, however, that there attaches to them a very great sentimental value in the hearts of all Canadians.
It has been shown in the history of the past as well as in recent history that, while nations may be ruled by politicians and statesmen, they are never aroused to action; they are never impelled to the doing of good deeds, until their hearts are touched and their sentiment aroused. I imagine, therefore, that in forwarding such a movement as this we shall be helping our fellow citizens and the growing generation to appreciate the better their responsibilities as Canadians. A study of the deeds of our ancestors; a contemplation of the difficulties which they underwent; a perusal of our history, will bring to our people and to the growing generation a love of country which will better fit us to assume our national status.
The history of these walls is truly remarkable-remarkable from the standpoint of the antiquarian as well as from the standpoint fMr. Power.]
of the historian; an object lesson to all of us; an object lesson to the growing generation-remarkable even from the standpoint of the soldier, because it shows that the art of defensive warfare has made wonderful strides within recent years.
In reviewing this history we may begin with the day when Champlain built at Quebec a rude stockade called "L'Habitation," fit only to repel the attacks of savages armed with bows and arrows, and go on' to the time when they built on the crest of the cliff a castle surrounded by a moat and a wall, called "Chateau St. Louis." Many of you may not know where the Chateau St. Louis was; its site will be more familiar to you when I tell you that it is that of the present Chateau Frontenac.
In the time of the Governor from whom the Chateau Frontenac takes its name, it was decided to enlarge the walls and spread them over a much greater area. This was done partly by the inhabitants themselves, who feared the growing power of the English colonists and their savage allies, and partly under the direction of the French kings, who realized that in Quebec they had the strategic point from which their possessions in New France might be defended. The work, however-like most Government work, I am sorry to say-was placed largely in the hands of contractors, and the contractors of that day resembled very much the contractors of our day. We read that short quantities of earth were delivered; that stones were mixed with sand; that works had to be repaired before they were completed. We read also that a certain amount of ingenuity was exercised in the carrying out of some of the schemes well known to our own modern political camp followers, such as change of plan, extras, and so on. Evidently they knew all these things in the days of Montcalm and Frontenac. However, we read also that in spite of these things, the military governors and engineers such as Frontenac, Montcalm, Denere, Delary, Franquert, Ponteroy and others undoubtedly were honest and did their best under adverse circumstances to make these walls safe against the invader. One thing, though, is certain: Wolfe's artillery men, though not armed with pieces of the heaviest weight even for that day, had no difficulty in effecting large breaches wherever they chose.
During the English regime, Murray when he was besieged by De Levis and later Sir Guy Carleton when he was besieged by continental troops, found that their sole defence against the invaders was the stout

heart of the defenders. We read also that in the letters of the governors of that time innumerable complaints were made to the home office of the insufficiency of the defences and that frequent requests were made for assistants, for men, for engineers, for materials, in order to strengthen the fortifications of that city which was the last bulwark of British dominion on the American continent. No comprehensive scheme, however, was entered into until 1823, when the walls were built which enclose approximately their present area. Later still, between 18601870 the experience of modern warfare having shown that the only means of defence for a city was to he found in separate and detached posts situated at some distance,- forts were constructed at Levis in a position commanding the river St. Lawrence. These forts have, I understand, proved to be of some utility during the recent war, and it is not my intention to ask that they be included in the plan which [DOT]I propose
It is not, however, so much the history of these bare walls and these crumbling stones to which I wish to direct the attention of the House to-day. I wish to emphasize the associations connected _ with them; to deal with a subject which certainly does not enter into the realm of practical politics and in connection with which there can certainly be nothing in the way of vituperation or recrimination. I hope that the House will bear with me for a few moments while I recall some of the events connected with these walls, and refer briefly to some of the men whose names are associated with them.
From the day in 1535 when Jacques Cartier, with a few scurvy-inflicted followers, entered the St. Charles river and wintered beside the Indian village of Stada-cona, down to the day when the mightiest Armada which had ever crossed the Atlantic, sailed up the St. Lawrence, bearing thirty-three thousand men who with their comrades were in four years to make known the word "Canada" in regions and to populations where hitherto it was considered almost as mythical as the fabled Atlantis; whose deeds stand out pre-eminent even in a war of giants; whose heroism has attracted the attention and praise of the nations of the earth through nearly four centuries-Quebec has been the spot on this hemisphere where history was made, where heroes lived and died, where a continent was lost and won. It was here that Champlain, a soldier, sailor and statesman,
first established a home and planted the Cross which was to bring to a continent the blessings of Christianity and civilization. From Quebec he set forth on those perilous journeys into unknown regions amongst unfriendly barbarous tribes which led to the discovery of the Ottawa river and the Great Lakes. Later he was succeeded by others of the same daring breed. Talon, Laval, Frontenac, al'l made their headquarters within these walls. Statesman and colonist, priest and educator, soldier and governor-all left on the colony the glamour of their personality and enriched our history by the shining examples which they have left to posterity. Talon, with the clear vision of genius, saw that a country hitherto popularly supposed to be useful only as an abode for criminals, adventurers and younger sons, or to be given over to the avaricious rapacity of the fur traders, could be made the home of a peaceful, happy populace, devoted to industry and the cultivation of the soil.
Laval, priest, founder and colonist, by a system of education, rendered this country at least to a certain extent independent of old France in arts, science, culture. By his firm insistence on the rights and privileges of the clergy, by his struggle on behalf of morality and. decency, he raised to a higher plane the standards of living which here as elsewhere had been lowered by the licentiousness and debaucheries of some of the wilder spirits. He instilled into the people of French Canada that love of authority, that God-fearing simplicity, and sense of moral responsibility which are the characteristics of the people of the province of Quebec to-day.
A little later Frontenac arrived, during the darkest hour of the colony. He subdued the Iroquois, terrorized the colonial settlements into an honourable truce and answered the imperious ultimatum of a British admiral anchored before the walls of Quebec by a haughty and successful reply from the mouth of his cannon. He put an end for a century to come to the menace of a British invasion of Quebec. Then later came priests and missionaries, the Recollects and Jesuits, trappers and explorers. They lived and struggled and died within the shadow of these mouldering walls. Time after time the Jesuits, unaccustomed to anything tout the best living in Europe, went out into uncharted country, faced death in a thousand horrible forms, and suffered martyrdom in order to bring to a new country the blessings of civilization. We must all recognize the courage of

the "coureur de bois," those hardy people who explored the Mississippi and were the first to discover our great West. Hon. members from the West should he glad to join with me in helping to reverence and perpetuate their memory by preventing the walls from which they started from falling into decay. Then came soldiers from Guinne and Picardy, descendants of whom are sitting around me in this Chamber today. These men must have viewed with gloomy foreboding the vast forests which lay before them. Little did they think that within a few centuries the trees whose shadows filled them with such a sombre feelmg would be utilized to make fortunes for thousands of people.
Later on, from his lookout perched high above Cape Diamond, Montcalm must have looked very sorrowfully down the St. Law renee at the mighty fleet containing the greatest force yet sent against the colony. He must have felt approaching the climax of the long struggle on the American continent between Briton and Gaul. Time does not permit me to dwell upon the trials and triumphs of the gallant Wolfe, nor upon the great battle of the Plains of Abraham, which so effectually decided the question of supremacy in Canada. Suffice it to say that the troops engaged were worthy foes, the reckless gallantry of France being matched by the calm courage and stubbornness of Britain. The prize, too, was worthy of the contest-the capture of the gateway to the northern portion of the American continent. The combat* was so fierce, even compared with modern warfare, that four brigadiers on one side and three on the other were either killed in action or died of wounds, and both officers commanding were mortally wounded whilst gallantly leading their men to the attack. So closely are the names of these two heroes associated, one over-shadowed in his last moments by defeat, and the other dying at the moment of victory, that a single monument has been erected to commemorate their glorious struggle.
The city was to be besieged again. The following year De Levis, having avenged France in a battle fought on almost the same grounds as the struggle of the previous year, sat down to starve Governor Murray and a few troops into submission. The garrison suffered incredible hardships throughout the winter, but with the spring came the eagerly awaited British fleet, and the British flag was seen unfurled to the breeze. French colonial policy then collapsed and England became possessor of the 
vast territories which now constitute the brightest gem in the diadem of the Empire.
Quebec was besieged once more in 1775. Continental forces had overrun the whole of Canada, till only Quebec City still remained free from the heel of the invader. Sir Guy Carleton, by his energy and ability, so stirred the inhabitants, bath English and French, that the city was put into such a state of defence that it withstood almost daily attacks from the forces of Arnold and Montgomery, till in the closing hours of 1775 the final assault was beaten off, and the bravest of the surviving Americans gave up his life attempting in vain to scale the cliffs.
Since that time, though the streets and squares have constantly echoed with the tramp of armed men, though the surrounding hills every day resound with the roar of artillery, no enemy has come within sufficient distance to give cause for alarm.
In another field, however, Quebec continued to be of the greatest importance to the Dominion. Here was staged the earliest debates on responsible government. Here was established for all time equal rights for the victor and vanquished in the matter of language and religion. Here sat the first Parliament of United Canada, and here, in 1864, were laid the foundation stones of our present Confederation.
In conclusion, let us remember that the facts which I have set forth are a large part of the history of all Canadians, no matter what their country of origin may be. The men whose deeds I have recalled are our common ancestors, and the newest Canadian as well as the descendant of fifty generations here, if he be proud of his country at all, should claim them and glory in their achievements and try to emulate them. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that no more befitting legislation could be adopted in the year of the opening of this magnificent new Parliament Building, which is a symbol of the growth into a mighty nation of the few provinces for whom these ancestors of ours laboured, fought and died, than to save from decay these crumbling walls in old Quebec, these mouldering stones, which witnessed their efforts on our common behalf.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Militia and Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which my hon. friend from South Quebec (Mr. Power) has just made brings to my attention for the first time this important question regarding the walls and fortifications of the ancient city of Quebec. When I first saw the notice on the Order Paper, I made inquiries in the department, but we

could find no record of any application having been made in the direction set out in the motion now before the House.
However, I have heard incidentally that Sir George Garneau, the Chairman of the Battlefields Commission, has asked some members of the Government that these walls and fortifications should be handed over to the Commission, and I may inform the House that at the present time the matter is under consideration by the Government and by the officials of the Department of Militia.
I must commend my hon. friend for the excellent manner in which he has brought this matter to the attention of the House in the motion which he has just moved, and also for the graceful, eloquent and charming recital which he has given to us of the history of the early days of this great country. I think many of us are far too prone to consider that the history of our common country begins about the year 1759, and far too many of us are either not informed, or else we forget that Canada has in reality a great history, an honourable history; a history adorned with all the colours of romance. From the year 1535, for nearly four centuries, perhaps the principle historic point of the whole country has been in and about the city of Quebec; and certainly not the least point of historic interest in that city, perhaps one of the most interesting of all, consists in the walls and the fortifications which originally were looked upon as an unconquerable stronghold, but which to-day under the conditions of modern warfare, would not be considered the slightest military importance. These fortifications, as I understand, came into possession of the Government of Canada under some express arrangements with the Imperial Government; but so far as my information goes, I do not think that there were any limitations whatever in the deed of gift or grant which would place any impediment in the way of the proposal to hand over these memorials to the Battlefields Commission. From the knowledge I possess of the matter-and I frankly admit that I am not very conversant with its details-I believe that the walls and fortifications are not now used for any military purpose and are not likely to be restored for such purpose by this or succeeding generations. The citadel itself is used for military purposes and troops are quartered there. The parade grounds are of course used, but the walls themselves and the fortifications connected therewith will not, I think, ever again be
of any practical use to the Government or the Department of Militia. During past years, I understand, some expenditure has been made in the work of restoration, both by the Department of Militia and Defence and by the Department of Public Works. Just what that expenditure amounts to I am not at the present moment able to state, but I know that within the last three months instructions have been issued to have a survey and report made of the whole situation in connection with these walls and fortifications; and I think that in the near future some scheme will be developed and a plan devised whereby conferences will be held between officials of the department and the Battlefields Memorial Commission in order that satisfactory arrangements may be made for the handing over of these walls and fortifications to that commission. Plans have not yet been fully developed in that respect; they are still under consideration by the department and the Government. Personally, I think there should be no hesitation in carrying out the plan suggested in this motion. I am very glad indeed that my hon. friend in moving the motion stated that he did not intend to press it at the present time but brought it forward to-day with the idea of presenting the matter directly to the attention of the Government and of this House. He has done more than that. He has put upon the pages of Hansard a charming address-
Hear, hear

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-which T have no
doubt will be very widely read in the schools and colleges of this country. He has given us a resume of Canadian history which will be of great value, and ho has clothed it in most charming language, simple and easy to understand. I think, therefore, he is entitled to the thanks as well as the congratulations of the House for the manner in which he has submitted his motion to day; and in adopting his suggestion to let the motion drop, I may assure him that the matter will be given the best of consideration of the Government.

I
have no desire to prolong the debate on this motion, but I wish to correct a wrong impression that seems to have possessed the House in regard to this matter. I have had some experience in going over fortifications, and I know how those of Quebec compare with other fortifications of similar character. The city of Ypres held out throughout the war. After the British took possession of its fortifications, it was never taken by the

whole force of the German army united against it on several occasions, the British army having found refuge in the casemates and the old crumbling walls of the city of Ypres. Now, the walls of Ypres were just as decrepit, and were in the same condition when the war broke out between Belgium and Germany, as are the walls of the city of Quebec at the present time. The city of Ypres was taken possession of by the army and the casemates were utilized, and other works of a temporary character were built with the walls, with the result that Ypres became impregnable. And had it not been for the manner in which that city was held there is no. doubt that the war would have ended in another way. The fortifications of Quebec as they stand to-day are far stronger and in a much better state of repair than were the fortifications of Ypres, and I have no hesitation in saying, as one who has seen the effect of war on the operation of fortifications of this kind, that any general who has had experience in defending fortresses in Europe would say that the form of the fortress of Quebec would lend itself to a defence that would be impregnable in any war that might occur in this country. Let us not make the mistake that these walls in Quebec are crumbled, ancient, and of no value. Behind them are rooms where men can go in casemates, which are far stronger and better than those in the city of Ypres. Th citadel of Quebec is impregnable under modern conditions. It is all very well to say that it could be blown up by artillery fire. Artillery might have some effect upon it-there is no doubt that it would have an effect upon it-but as to blowing it up or putting it out of business as a military stronghold, it cannot be done. For that reason the Government would be ill-advised to withdraw the garrison from the citadel and to remove the Quebec fortifications. The nature of the city, and of the fortifications of Quebec assure the protection of the St. Lawrence with the guns we have now. With some of those great howitzers which we have seen in Ottawa no enemy could come up the St. Lawrence beyond a point twenty miles from the city of Quebec. Before the war it was a common saying that the Canadian army was insignificant. People used to sneer at our soldiers and at the fortifications and armament of Quebec. In spite of all that, when the real, acid test of the war came the Canadian soldier was found to be just as good as any other soldier in the world and as far as the First Division was concerned its guns and its armament filled a gap in the life of the war but for which I 
doubt whether history would have been written in the way it is to-day.
Nobody knows what a day may bring forth. We even now have nations rattling the sword at Canada and trying to give us a little taste of their frightfulness. We may have trouble and we must be prepared for the next five or ten years to take our place in the ranks with our British brethren in case trouble comes to Canada or to the Empire. For that reason, instead of tearing down the fortifications of Quebec and w'ith-dkayring entirely the garrison from the city, we should maintain the fortifications in good order and keep the garrison there. The garrisoning of the city is so important to the protection of the St. Lawrence that I would strongly urge upon the Government to have a commission of Imperial engineers, men, who have had experience of fortifications during the war, to go over the works and see what can be done with them. Walls of a poorer character in the city of Ypres withstood the full force of the greatest German guns and offered refuge for the British soldiers throughout the war. The riding school in Ypres, which was built with great underground places as refuges fop soldiers, two hundred or three hundred years ago, served as a refuge for British soldiers during the war. The ancient engineers who built these walls and the men who built fortresses of the same character as that at Quebec understood their business very well and the modern engineer has not been able to improve very much upon their work. They knew liow to build fortifications. There are old text books on fortifications which were used in the time of Marlborough and their teachings are still good to-day.
Amongst other nations the fortress at Quebec is looked upon as one of the great fortresses of the British Empire and it would be a mistake if the impression were to go forth that Canada was about to dismantle a fortress which is impregnable. At Halifax another great fortress stands overlooking the Atlantic ocean. For the purposes of war and defence the fortifications at Quebec are just as modern as any fortifications that could be designed to-day. All you would have to add would be outworks in the form of earthwork which could be done at any time in -a day or two. I hope the impression will not go abroad, or that the Minister of Militia will not gain the impression, from the remarks which have fallen -from the hon. member for Quebec city (Mr. Power), that the fortress at Quebec is useless, because there is no

better design to-day in so far as the citadel is concerned than that to be found at Quebec. Passages and galleries might be added underground but otherwise the works are perfect. The great engineers who designed that fortress knew how to construct * work of that character and the fortress is just as modem to-day as the bayonet is still a useful weapon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. member for Quebec South rises to speak I must remind hon. members that he is exercising his right to close the debate and if any other member desires to speak he should do so now.

A word only in answer to my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie.) I make no pretention of being a military authority as he is and therefore I do not intend to discuss with him the question as to whether or not these works are useless in time of war. All I can tell him is that that seems to have been the impression of the Militia Department.-
None of them have gone to war.

Nor is it the impression of one who is not a member of the Militia Department and who has gone to war. I wish to tell the hon. member that I put in a year at Ypres and I never saw a casemate or a wall there-I was in the trenches.
You could not have been in the hospital at the Menin Gate if you did not see one.

I shall close the debate and not enter into any recriminations. I shall withdraw the resolution on the assurance of the minister that this matter is receiving the attention of the Government and that an investigation of the whole ques-ion will be made. That will no doubt be satisfactory even to the hon. member for North Simcoe.
Motion withdrawn.
