speakeroldname: Mr. CHARLES GAVIN POWER (Quebec South) moved:
speechtext:
That, In the opinion ot this House, it is expedient to amend the Act to provide Pensions to or in respect ot Members of the Canadian Naval and Military Air Forces, 1919, so as to provide that the pension of a widowed mother of a Member of the Forces who has died on active service shall not be reduced on account of her income ; and further that Pension shall he granted her of right whether or not there are other living children.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a long way from the musty walls of the Quebec fortifications and the heroes of ancient Canadian history to the heroes of our own day and their dependents. I doubt whether I would have undertaken the task of discussing this matter had I not seen in his seat my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn) who has always been very much interested in it from the same standpoint as I have been. Section 34, if I remember rightly, of the new Pensions Act allows, a pension to the dependent widowed mother of a soldier killed in action. If she is not in receipt of any income the full amount of the pension is granted to her. Previously to last year should she have been in receipt of any earnings whatsoever the amount of these earnings were deducted from her total pension. To give you a concrete example: "Supposing a widowed mother is entitled to a pension of $600 a year, and that, as a washerwoman in one of the departments she earned $300 a year. Well, this was deducted from her pension; the Government paid her only $300. This obvious injustice was remedied last year in the Pension Act of 1919, but there still remains another injustice:	We
have deliberately excluded from the provisions of this amendment the widowed mother who is in receipt of an income of any kind-an income in stocks, bonds, pensions, insurance, et cetera-and we have left this matter entirely to the discretion of the Board of Pension Commissioners in cases of what they call extreme hardship. Now what I maintain is this: The widowed mother, whoever she may be, is as much entitled to the pension of right as the wife; that in many cases, in a large number of cases in fact, the mother is more entitled to a pension than the wife. The wife in a good number of cases may marry again, whereas the widowed mother is very often past that age-past the age where she may earn a living to augment her pension, and in such a position that she practically becomes an object of public charity. So that it is my contention that the widowed mother of a soldier should be allowed to obtain the same amount of pension whether she has or has not any income. We have heard in this House-I do not wish to revive old controversies because too much was heard of the matter last year-arguments with regard to the unmarried wife and respecting, as my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council would say "the wife by habit and repute." That I think was the last phrase we arrived at during the debate in question.

I do not wish to again revive the question of the wife "by habit and repute" but I imagine that the widowed mother of a soldier is more entitled to a tpension than this wife by habit and repute. Let me cite a concrete case which I brought up in the House on a previous occasion, namely, the case of a young man, a barrister, who went away to the war as a private soldier, his people being well-to-do. During the war his father died leaving his mother not quite well off. Meanwhile the boy had attained the rank of Captain. He was killed and the widowed mother was granted a sum of $66 per month. About a year, or perhaps two years, after she had been in the enjoyment of this pension, what is termed " a visiting officer" called upon her and inquired whether she was being well treated. The lady was thankful for the $66 per month and told the visitor that everything was quite satisfactory, and that the Government had treated her very well. Then the lady visitor inquired "Have you any other resources?" " Oh, yes, I have a house in the country and I get $300 a year from that." " I see, $300." Deduct that from $800 and it leaves $500.	" Have you got anything
else?" " Yes, I draw $100 a year from insurance." Take that off also, making a total deduction of $400. This lady is left with $400 from the Government and her only son, that was her support and but for the war would now be earning a good income, has given up his life at the front. The age of this lady is such that she is utterly incapable of earning her living, and is practically left on the country. I maintain, sir, that in justice and fairness the widowed mother should be placed in the same position as the wife and no deduction of income should be made whatsoever. If the son has died at the front the widowed mother should get a pension just as when the husband dies at the front the wife gets a pension. We have debated this question before the Committee on Pensions and on two or three occasions we almost carried the point. We have not succeeded so far, and therefore I have deemed it my duty to bring the matter before the attention of the House.

As the mover of the resolution has stated I have been much interested in this question, and he and I throughout the consideration of the Pension Bill fought strongly for more favourable treatment to widowed mothers. Wo were unfortunately in a minority in the Pension Committee, and when we renewed our struggle in the House an amendment

was suggested to the Pension Act which I, at least, thought would have given relief. That amendment was dropped at the request of the minister in charge of the Bill. H my memory serves me right it was declare-:1 not to be in order for a private member f[. propose a resolution which involved the expenditure of public money; but there was another reason for delaying the amendment; it was hoped to get some information from the Pensions Board which would tell us just how much the proposed ' change would involve in the way of expenditure. From that time to this I have not heard whether that information was forthcoming, and as I did not know until this afternoon that the resolution was to be discussed I am not very well prepared to speak on the several points in issue. However, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Power) has explained, the widowed mother who is in receipt of an independent income from any source has deducted from her pension, which she would otherwise be entitled to, the amount of that income, and this, as he says, works very great hardship in certain cases.
On a former occasion I mentioned a concrete case of the sort where the widow of a clergyman, entitled to an annuity of $300, had for some time received a pension of $480 because of the death of her son at the front. Later on, under the regulations embodied in the Act, that $300 of annuity was deducted, and she received only $180 by way of pension. Other hon. members have similar cases arising in their own constituencies and these were also set out. Objection was raised that this was, in a manner, class legislation-that a widowed mother might be in receipt of so large an income that it would be absurd to further augment her living allowance. But that is easily guarded against if the amendment suggested were to be adopted. We could easily provide that if a widowed mother received a larger sum than her entire pension she would only be entitled to a certain amount. But even if it is class legislation I appeal to you, Sir, and to the House, that of all people in the world mothers should be entitled to a preference.
The mover of the resolution has made mention of the discussion with regard to unmarried wives. I know I was struck at that time by the objection made to the phraseology, which we of a somewhat coldblooded race saw at first no reason against adopting. The objection was all the more curious too, because in the English language we have one word for wife and another for

woman, whereas my friends from Quebec use but the one word femme to denominate either a woman or a wife.
Now, I venture to appeal to both sides of this House on behalf of an even more sacred person than the wife-I appeal on behalf of the mother. For that reason alone I would urge, without going further into the matter, favourable consideration of the resolution moved by the member for Quebec (Mr. Power).

Mr. Speaker, I am heartily in accord with the resolution which has been moved by the member for Quebec (Mr. Power). As hon. members who have spoken on the resolution have said, this matter has been discussed by the Pensions Committee for the last two years. Last year we made a move along this line; that is, we said that when the mother earned any money by work it should not be deducted from her pension. This resolution goes one step further and asks us to state that if she has a private income it shall not be deducted from her pension. But all mothers are not included; the privilege is asked only for widowed mothers.
I am sure that nothing in connection with the Pension administration creates more difficulties, more misunderstandings and in many cases a feeling of greater injustice than the existing rule. As has been pointed out, it is necessary that in each case an investigator should make minute inquiries as to the properties or moneys which these ladies-usually aged-have, and often the investigators do not get the facts right, and in scarcely any case are they able to impress upon the people to whom they go the difference between them and some other widowed mother who perhaps lives in the same community. Consequently the impression is created that we aie rather small, that the shades of difference we draw are perhaps what might be termed picayune. If it is a matter of money, one might point out that most of these widowed mothers are advanced in years, and the pensions will continue only during the remainder of their lives.
Last year the Great War Veterans and others came to us and asked for a gratuity for able-bodied soldiers. Our general answer was:	"No, we do not believe in
the principle of giving money to able-bodied men, because what money we intend to spend we wish to reserve for the dependents of soldiers." Now, I do not think there is any class more deserving than the widowed
mother. We are only asking that she get the same consideration as the widow of the soldier, and we are limiting it to the widowed mother. Having regard to the attitude which we took last year, to the present rules which are not entirely satisfactory, and to the arguments which have been advanced by hon. members, and also to my study of the matter and my knowledge of it gained by contact with these people during the last few years, I have no hesitation in recommending this reform which in justice to the class concerned we cannot longer delay.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to associate
myself with my hon. friend the mover of this resolution and with those hon-. members who have supported it. I had not the privilege of being present at the meetings of the Committee that spent so much time in discussing and studying this question of pensions, but I have had some experience of it in connection with requests that have been made to me on behalf of widowed mothers, which requests I have taken up with the Pensions Department.
One of the strongest cases brought to my notice was that of a woman who had two sons overseas. Her husband was sick, and on one of her sons being killed in action a pension was given to the family. Finally the husband died, and after some investigation the pension was withdrawn from the widowed mother, on the ground that she had another son who was morally bound to support her-although he did not do so. If that is the proper ruling under the Pension Act, Mr. Speaker, I submit it ought to be changed so that the widowed mother may not have to depend upon charity, but may have that support by way of pension which her sacrifice richly entitles her to.

Mr. Speaker, I have very
strong opinions in regard to the subject matter of this resolution. I was not one of the committee that dealt with pensions, although I appeared before them on two or three occasions pressing for more liberality of treatment. Coming from a city that furnished between 5,000 and 6,000 men to the overseas forces, I feel that I have a good deal of experience in dealing with the classes that come within the scope of this resolution. I have had similar cases to the one just mentioned by the member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) and some, I think, even stronger than that, and my heart has been pained and I have been actually almost

forced to tears listening to the widows' tales of their struggles to keep their families going. I do not know whether my letters will ever see the light of day, but during the last two or three years I have written the very strongest letters I am capable of to the Pension Commissioners, pointing out the cases of gross injustice which have been brought to my attention. Whether the treatment of such cases is in accordance with the regulations or not, I do not think that we as a country can afford to allow it to exist as undoubtedly it does exist at the present time. It continues after this committee dealt with it so exhaustively last year. Within the last few weeks I have had one or two cases brought before me, and I am going to give one, Mr. Speaker, in order that you may see how the Act works.
I cite the case of a widow who at the beginning of the war had a husband and two sons. The eldest son enlisted first and served almost throughout the war:	He was practically the
mainstay of the family before he went away and would have been so on his return. He served for upwards of four years, but in the closing days of the war he was killed. The second son went over later, and was severely wounded, his leg being shattered from the knee down. After both sons had gone the husband came home from a recruiting meeting and said to his wife: " There is still an appeal for men; they are wanted at the front; I feel that it is my duty to go." Though upwards of fifty years of age he volunteered for service and was accepted. On account of some trouble with his feet he never got overseas but he did serve at the Niagara frontier for a year or two. During that service he became inflicted with a trouble which, though not originating during service, was aggravated to such an extent that he had to be discharged and shortly afterwards died. Up to the present time that man's widow has received no pension. She lost her husband in the service or as a result of the service; her eldest son was killed at the front after more than four years of the most strenuous fighting, and the third boy, who had his leg shattered, came home and was able to qualify as a telegraph operator at a very good remuneration, I admit,

$90 a month. Well, this is what the Pension Board gave him; in respect of that permanent injury to a limb he is getting $4 a month by way of pension, the limitation of amount being on the ground that he was able to earn $90 a month as telegraph operator. The Pension Board also told him to hand over
1 M r. Coclcshuttl
to his widowed mother $10 a month to help her to live. Now, I have in black and white from the Pension Board what is virtually an admission of these facts; and I say that my blood boils to think that this country can do no better for a widow than that. I know the facts in this case; I have submitted them to the Pension Board just as strongly as I am submitting them now, but I have failed to get any redress for that widow. She told me with tears in her eyes that she could not support her remaining children and herself under these conditions. The young man whose limb has been shattered is engaged to be married, and the final intimation I got from the Pension Board was that if the young man would get married they would consider the widow's case on its merits and that probably she would get some pension. I know of other cases of the same kind; if one son is left at home, the widow cannot get a pension. This country owes a duty to that widow who gave her husband and her sons in the great conflict; she should not be treated on a charitable basis. I understand that the widow of whom I speak has two other children at home. One of them is a boy of fifteen-he is not strong and may be in poor health for at least a number of years-the other is a boy of seven. This is not an isolated case; cases of this kind, I believe, are fairly common throughout the country. I know of another case where four sons out of five sustained casualties out of the war, two being killed and two wounded and because the widow had one son left she was told that there was no pension coming to her. I know of another case, a widow who is able to work in a bank. She has moved from Brantford to New Brunswick and is now in the constituency of the member for York-Sunbury (Mr. H. P. McLeod). He and I have done all we could during a period of two or three years to get the case of this widow considered by the Pension Board, but because she is able to earn something by working in the bank she has not been given a pension. The Pension Board evidently arrived at this decision by deducting the amount she earns from the amount to which she would otherwise be entitled by way of pension. This business of reducing the pension by this amount and by that until it is whittled down to nothing is carried on to such an extent that I really wonder why, on that basis and according to their argument, the Pension Board did not actually find the widow to be in debt to the country. In my judgment the -whole thing has been

carried on from the wrong point of view. When a family have sacrificed husband, father or son, they have placed this country under an obligation, and that obligation is to see that want does not enter the house in which that family lives. It does not matter whether or not there is a prospect of help coming later. It is not fair to say that the members of a family must always stay in their old home until the parent is dead. I know three or four cases of young men who are engaged but who are obliged to stay at home practically as long as the mother lives. They dare not get married on the strength of the supposition that the Government will do the right thing, because they are afraid ' that the Government are not going to do the right thing in regard to pension. While we have treated our soldiers with the utmost liber-dity :n Connection with practically every service which they have rendered, when it comes to the matter of pension there is, for some reason, a kink in the system; they are not treated in a humane manner. I have had long experience in connection with pensions and have dealt with a very large variety of cases; and I can say that the Pension Board are either tied up by red tape or by regulations.
I have another grievance against the Pension Board in the way the pensions are administered. After a member has struggled hard-and it is a hard struggle to get anything like justice done by the Pension Board-I say, after a member has struggled hard, and has finally obtained a fairly satisfactory settlement for a widow, it may happen that the payments go on for three cr six months and then you are suddenly wakened up with a jolt to find that the same thing has been undone. I have had that occur time and again. Now, in my judgment, after a thorough investigation has been made and a pension supposedly decided upon as final, it should not be open to the Pension Board to go back on the arrangement that has been made and to throw the whole thing into the air again as has been done time and again. I could mention names, but I do not think it is wise; I do not want to drag them into the publicity that the mention of them would give. But I know of cases where twice over a pension has been cut down, without any apparent reason, after having been, to all intents and purposes, finally settled and arranged between the Pension Board and the family on the basis of a thorough investigation. I say that this country is well enough off, badly as
it has been hit by the war, to take care of all those who should receive pensions, The department, or whoever is responsible should limber up considerably, and not simply consider to what extent the Pension Bill for the year would be raised by appropriate action, but whether justice is being done to the individals and families they are dealing with. If it is found that justice is not being done and that the families have not enough to live on, I contend that it is the duty of this Government to set that matter right. The question my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn) has raised is one that has often tripped me up when I have been trying to get pension cases settled. It will suddenly be discovered by the board or by some visitor who is mighty inquisitive, that the pensioner has a little income from somewhere, it does not matter where, and the pension is at once cut down by that amount.
I had one case recently where the board discovered that a widow, living in Brantford, who had been receiving a pension, I think, of $600 a year, owned two houses in Toronto. The rent of one house was $12 a month, and of the other approximately the same-about $25 a month from the two. When this fact was discovered by some inquisitive visitor, would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, the board deducted the whole amount pf the rent from the $600 pension which the widow had been receiving for some little time, without making any allowance whatever for repairs, insurance, or even taxes. The whole rental from the two houses was deducted from the original pension, and I had to put up a considerable fight, which I did, before I got this injustice remedied. While the pension was not restored to its original amount, I did succeed in showing the board that it was not very business-like to assume, because a certain amount of rental is supposed to come in from a house, that it always does come in. Every hon. member knows that even if it does come in, there are a lot of other things to be considered, such as repairs, taxes and insurance, and the house may be empty for two or three or even six months. But simply because a widow has a house that is supposed to bring in a rental of $12 a month, the policy of the board is to deduct that amount as if she had the rental already in her pocket. The thing is absurd from a business standpoint, because rent for a house is not in your pocket until the cheque has been honoured by the bank, and then there are these deductions I have spoken of.

I hope this question will come up again. I do not think this will be the finish of it. I do not know whether the hon. member for South Quebec (Mr. Power) thinks it will be the finish of it if we pass this resolution. What we want is action. In spite of what was done by the committee last year I cannot take back anything I have said. I tried then to speak as strongly as words would permit in favour of proper treatment for the soldier and his dependents. Whether all the committee's recommendations are in full operation or not, I do not know, but I have certainly had some very severe cases since the regulations wrere put into effect last year. I have mentioned one case, and I could give others. In my judgment it is a shame that widows with dependent children who have lost a husband, or son, or brother in the war, who was their chief support, cannot have their cases treated in a reasonable way.
Furthermore, under the present regulations the woman who tries to help herself is penalized. The Government practically says that she should not have any income from any other source, and that if she has, they will deduct that amount from her pension. I say the country either owes these women a debt or it does not, and it is most unjust to make these deductions simply because a widow may have $200 or $300 or $500 coming in from a piece of property, to acquire which she has had to scrape for years. The pensions are much too small at the best, and are miserable at the worst. I am ashamed to mention the $3 or $4 pension. I have mentioned the case of a boy permanently disabled who receives a pension of only $4 a month. I say that if this Government cannot give a better pension than that to one who is permanently lame, it should not give anything. I would be ashamed to dole out such a small amount. I contend that this matter should be gone into thoroughly, and that every case of injustice should be considered on its merits by some competent authority. I know that there are some who will try to get out of the department more than they are entitled to receive, but don't let us think everybody is a robber; don't let us do an injustice to an innocent person because somebody else is trying to get a few dollars more than they should have. I am confident that the pensions that are being paid to the disabled soldier, to the widow and orphans, or whoever it may be that has suffered, will none of them be found to be over-generous, and a great many of them will be found to be entirely

inadequate. At the risk of raising our pension bill five or ten millions per annum, I say this country owes it to itself and to its citizens to see that a grave injustice is not done to the widow and the orphan. I speak strongly because I feel strongly. I have been almost moved to tears in my office time and again by the relation of the facts alone, and I have felt that I ought to put my hand in my pocket and pay the pensions myself rather than let the poor widow go out of my office as she has had to go. I urge the House as strongly as I can to take active and adequate steps this session to see that the injustices I have spoken of do not continue any longeer.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with other hon. members in supporting the resolution moved by the hon. member for South Quebec (Mr. Power). I have had a number of cases in my county and town of the nature described by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp). The widowed mother of a soldier who has given his life for Canada and the Empire should be entitled to receive her full pension, no matter what her circumstances may be at any time. I have had a case where a pension was refused to a widow because she had a son who had reached the age of eighteen. He had never been able to earn a living for himself, because he was not physically strong enough to do hard work, and did not have the education to do other than manual work. In another case, a widowed mother was refused a pension because she had a son living in the United States or in some distant part of Canada who had been away from home for years and years and was unwilling to assist in supporting her. I also know' of cases where a certain amount of the pension has been deducted because there have been other sources of income. One widowed mother had been receiving a pension of $60 a month for a year or two-her son had been a captain-and then it was discovered that she was the owner of two or three acres of land from which she got a certain revenue, and her pension was reduced to $30 a month. After consideration* of the circumstances, and as a result of representations made by myself, the commissioners raised the pension to $45. I am convinced that the commissioners themselves are in sympathy with the mothers and dependents of the soldiers, but they are precluded from the exercise of any generosity by reason of the regulations. I therefore join with other

hon. members in urging Parliament at this session to take such action as will effectively remedy the present unsatisfactory condition of affairs and give to the widowed mothers of the soldiers adequate consideration. There are very few wealthy women among the Canadian widowed mothers of soldiers, and we could not, I should imagine, be much worse off if we spent a substantial sum of money in granting them proper relief than we should be if the war had been lost. Let Canada show her generosity to those who made the supreme sacrifice, not only for her own safety but for the freedom of men the world over and for the honour of the Empire.

I desire to point out to my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) that under the regulations no deduction is made in the case of a woman who is earning money. A man's pension is based strictly on the degree of his incapacity through service to earn a living in the ordinary labour market; and his pension having been once fixed, no deduction is afterwards made by reason of anything which he may earn outside.

My hon. friend says that no deduction is made. Well, I can mention a case where nothing was ever granted and therefore nothing could be deducted. The case I mentioned from Fredericton is that of a widow who has now lost her only son, and because she is earning money in a bank her case has not been adjusted or even considered by the Pensions Board.
If she is earning money by her own effort it is not deducted from the pension she is entitled to.
But she does not get any.

I cannot help that. So far as the Pensions Board is concerned, my hon. friend from Brantford and others must bear in mind that it is an administrative body. The board is appointed to administer the Act, and if there is anything wrong with the Act itself it is for this House to adjust the irregularity. It is the duty of my hon. friend from Brantford, if a committee is appointed this year, to bring before it the cases he speaks of.
I have already appeared twice before the committee.

If he does so, I do not think there is one member of the committee
who will not assist him to have matters adjusted. Let me say, however, that I have never had to write a second letter to the board over any matter whatever after having once told them the exact facts, and having acted in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Pensions Board cannot vary the Act any more than I, as a private member, can. They have to be bound by the regulations, and I think it is most unfortunate to blame them for doing properly what they consider to be their duty. My experience lia^ been entirely satisfactory with the board, and any question on which I have written them they have endeavoured to attend to in accordance with the regulations laid down in the Act.
You had more influence.
I had no influence whatever.

The present discussion is one of very great importance to widowed mothers. Only last Saturday I received a telegram from an organization which is new to me, the Organized Mothers and Widows, in which they specifically called attention to the matter now under discussion. I do not think that this subject is at all new to any honourable member, for all of us, I have no doubt, have questions of one kind or another brought to our attention in relation to the position of widowed mothers who are in receipt of pensions, or should receive consideration. It was pointed out to me, on investigation, that the little change which I have suggested would cost the country $5,000,000. Hon. members will realize the necessity for the appointment of a committee of some kind to go into these matters. On the Order Paper there will be found a suggestion, which T trust will come before the House on Wednesday, that a committee should be appointed on the subject, which I think it is eminently desirable should be inquired into. I must agree with my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Nesbitt) that the Pension Board is purely administrative, and I have found its members always very fair. But the fact that the matter I have suggested would cost $5,000,000 is, I think, ample evidence of its importance to the hon. members of this House. The pension, as far as I understand the matter, is based on the principle that no widowed mother shall have less than a living if she has lost her support by the war. If there are two women living side by side receiving, say $48 a month, and one is allowed to receive an income of $500, or $600,



or $700 a year, while the other has no opportunity to augment her pension, there might very well arise antagonism to what is commonly called " class legislation." To my mind, Mr. Speaker, the solution of the problem lies in raising the entire pension rate, which at the present time is too low.

I rise to support the motion, as I have risen repeatedly in this House to express my sympathy with the mothers and widows Of men who served their country in the late struggle. I shall not delay the Efouse at this time with any lengthy discussion of the question, because I think that enough has been said. I am convinced that the Government have not closed the door upon any questions appertaining to the returned soldiers, and I think my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) has expressed that determination. I have no doubt the time will come when the Government will appreciate the advisability of affording to this House an opportunity to discuss the subject from all possible standpoints. If, however, they do not grant that opportunity, then we shall bring the matter up in some other manner. I am sure they will give us a chance to go thoroughly into the question, for as I said before, and said advisedly, I rely on this Government to do everything humanly possible on behalf of the soldiers and the widowed mothers. I do not see within sight any other prospective Government that will be willing to do any more than this Government has done or can do. The very first question in regard to the soldiers should be that of pensions. I made this statement in my constituency; that the widows and orphans of the men, our comrades, who were left over on the battlefields of France and Flanders, should be given first consideration. I will not recite the case which I have in mind, but I may assure the House that there are many which should receive eveiy consideration. I think the whole subject could be more advantageously discussed at a later date; and, as I have said before, I am convinced that the Government will grant an opportunity to discuss the question of pensions. We shall therefore await with anxiety their decision on the question, and if they can not grant ample opportunity to go into the matter then I shall take steps to bring it before the House.
Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Caileton):	Assuredly the question
under discussion is one in which every man in this country is deeply interested; and while the motion has reference to pensions

for widowed mothers, perhaps there are others who come within its scope with greater urgency and reason. I have in mind the case of a soldier in my constituency who at the age of 47 enlisted within a week of the outbreak of war. He was overseas two years and was severely gassed, returning home on the ship that took his three sons back to England to serve their country. That man was so anxious to return to civil life that he did not apply for a pension at that time, notwithstanding his severe suffering from the effects of gas. He was one of the old fellows who had considerable sand in him, and he would do a man's work, in spite of every obstacle or hardship which he could possibly surmount. In a very short time, however, his privations at the front told upon him and he had to go under medical treatment. He was sent to a medical hospital in St. John where he developed tuberculosis as the result of the weakening of his lungs from gassing. He was granted a pension of $5.50 a month at first, and after he had been in the hospital six months the doctors pronounced him 100 per cent disabled and he was granted a total disability pension. His case was reconsidered, however, and to-day he is receiving $5.50 a month. He has a family of three small children, one being an invalid, and the mother's time and care are taxed to their utmost. They have a home which they are in imminent danger of losing if they cannot meet the payments on it. This unfortunate man is at present in a military hospital, totally unable to do anything. The doctor has informed him that if he had come to the hospital when he was first discharged there would have been a fair chance of his recovery; but to-day, I regret to say, his condition is such that it is only a question of prolonging life. His pension was cut down on the ground that too long a time had elapsed from the date of his discharge to the time of his being pronounced totally disabled. I must say very emphatically, Mr. Speaker, that it would be an everlasting disgrace to this country if a man who had given such service, and whose family had given such service to their country were not granted an adequate pension to support his family, no matter what might be the cause of his disability. At the last special session of Parliament, I think, there was a sum of $40,000,000 voted for the patriotic purpose of supporting needy soldiers through the winter. In the early part of the winter this family applied for aid, and although

the man's certificate was filled up by two physicians, one who originally attended him, and another, the military doctor appointed in the town in which he lived, both of whom pronounced him 100 per cent disabled, the chairman of the local board refused to sign the necessary papers authorizing the payment of aid to his family. This soldier applied to me and I went to the chairman of the Patriotic Fund Committee and told him that I wanted him to either sign that paper or give me a written statement of his reasons why he would not sign. He said the reason he would not sign was because there were three grown up sons. These sons had been overseas from 1916 until peace was declared when they came home and were demobilized. They are seeking to re-establish themselves and I think you will all agree with me that these men have a right to their own earnings to re-establish themselves after giving three years to the service of their country. The chairman of the Patriotic Fund Committee did sign this paper but he said "I will see that they do not get anything." I do not know what steps he took but I imagine he wrote to the authorities here not to pay the money. These boys are endeavouring to make the payments on their house. Here is this woman, worse than a widow, with three small children, one of them an invalid, getting $5.50 a month and nothing from the Patriotic Fund. I appeal to the members of this House if they think that is the way Canada should discharge her obligations to her soldiers. The man who is killed is out of his misery but this poor man is suffering untold agony and cannot at the best live very long.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Council) :
speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Two questions have been brought up this afternoon entirely distinct-one of the law and the other of the administration of the law. The Board of Pension Commissioners are in no way responsible for the law. That was made by this House. It is their duty to administer the law as this Parliament made it. I was glad to hear the remarks of the hon. members for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon,) the hon. member for Winnipeg Centre (Mr. Andrews) and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) in appreciation of the work of the Board of Pension Commissioners. No doubt they are fallible as all other men are but they are all men who have served overseas. They are all men who, I am sure, have the deepest sympathy with the returned men and their dependents and I, am sure I am but speaking the truth when 28i
I say that they are exceedingly anxious to administer the law as they understand it in the way which will do justice to those who are entitled to have the benefit of the pension regulations. The Pension Commissioners are a body entirely independent of the Government but I feel that it is due to them in their absence to say 4his much in reference to their work. As to the law, the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is correct in his statement of the position. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) is possibly not aware that last year we changed the law on the point he mentioned. Prior to the amendment of the law last year the earnings of a widow were deducted when the question of her pension came to be decided but the law was changed last year so that the earnings of a widow are no longer taken into account.

I mentioned the
specific case that I had taken up myself three or four times where a widow was earning $700 or $800 a year working in a bank. Her case would not be considered so long as she was working in the bank.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Either my hon. friend is misinformed as to the situation or the Board of Pension Commisioners are misinformed. Up to September 1 last year that was the law and the Board of Commissioners were bound to administer it but that has not ibeen the law since the 1st of September and the Board of Pension Commissioners have (been administering the law on the other basis since, because an actual case which they had before them came under my observation-
The case to which 1 refer may have been righted within the last two or three months.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has been lighted since the 1st of September because it was on that date that the law passed, last session came into force. Therefore the point that my hon. friend raises with reference to a widow's earnings is no longer a matter requiring our consideration. Take the other question, the one brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), supported by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) and other members of the House, and which, I am sure, is one that commands the sympathy of every one in the House. We are all deeply interested in the welfare of the widows who have lost their sons and we are all anxious that no injustice shall be done to them. I think however that I should state to the House the position in

which this matter stood last session, particularly in view of the observations of my hon. friend from London. The members of the House will recall that for two sessions-that is in the session of 1918 and the spring session of 1919-we had a committee composed of members from both sides which wept very fully into the question of our pension law. The committee reported its findings to the House and the Government in each case accepted its conclusions -as to what the pension regulations should be in the first case, and as to what the pension law should be in the second.
This particular matter was considered at length by the committee. The hon. member from Quebec (Mr. Power) and the hon. member from London (Mr. Cronyn) pressed their view upon the committee with great force.' A substantial number of the members of the committee sympathized with the view presented, but when it came to a vote the majority was against that view for reasons which perhaps it is not at all necessary to enter into now. It is true that the hon. member for London raised the question on the floor of the House and submitted an amendment differing somewhat from the motion which my hon. friend (Mr. Power) had submitted. The latter, if accepted, would place a widow who might have a fortune of one, two or three hundred thousand dollars in the position to receive a pension just the same as the widow who is left with practically no means of support. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for London was not the same. It recognized a limited income, and in the case of a limited income provided that it should not be taken into account in fixing the pension. I did state to the House when the hon. member proposed his amendment that I would ascertain the facts from the Board of Pension Commissioners as to how much it would cost the country if the amendment were accepted, and if the Government could see its way clear to accept the amendment I might suggest that it be introduced into the Senate. I was under the impression that I had informed the member for London of the result of that investigation. The result was this: We found that accepting the hon. gentleman's amendment would involve an additional charge upon the revenues of the country of between two and three millions- I think about three millions a year. Possibly adopting the amendment proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Power) now might involve the charge that the member for Winnipeg has mentioned-five millions. The view of the Government last session was

that as the Pension Committee had considered the matter in all its bearings at great length, and had reached the conclusions which had been reported to the Ho'use, and as the House had accepted that report in Committee of the Whole, the wisest course for the Government was to act on the Pensions Committee's report, is it had always done, and leave this matter over for consideration when the Pension Committee was formed this year.
I want to say to the hon. member for Quebec (Mr. Power) it is the intention of the Government that there should be a Committee on Pensions this year, just as there has been at prior sessions of the House, and already a Government notice of motion is on the Order Paper for the appointment of such a committee. That is necessary because my hon. friend will recall that under the law as passed last year the bonus only continues until the first of September next, and the committee must review the question as to whether that bonus is to be continued, or modified, or made permanent. A number of other important questions relating to the matter will also be required to be considered. Therefore I suggest to my hon. friend that this motion -on a matter of great importance and commanding the sympathy of members of the House-should be referred to the Committee on Pensions when appointed, for consideration and a report to the House by that committee in connection with other matters that will come up.
I will not occupy very long in replying to the minister-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 should point out to the House that if the hon. gentleman exercises his right to reply, the debate on this resolution will be closed. Therefore if any other hon. member desires to speak on the question he now has an opportunity.

It was far from my intention, in presenting this resolution, to reflect in any manner whatsoever on the Board of Pension Commissioners. I know the three commissioners personally and I have always received the kindest treatment and courtesy at their hand. A reading of the resolution itself should make it clear that my object is to amend the law in order to place beyond dispute who is, and who is not entitled to have a pension under Article 34. I have in mind two cases recited to me by the former hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) last year. For example, supposing a boardinghouse keeper were earning $40 a month from her boarding-house and suddenly

wished to change that boarding-house into an apartment-house, her earnings would then become income and she would lose her pension. I want this kind of thing stopped once and for all so that the widowed mother of a soldier will get a pension even if she has $300,000 just as the wife of a soldier sometimes has $300,000. If she does not want to apply for the pension she need not do so; but I want every widowed mother to be entitled to the pension, and that is the object I had in proposing this resolution. However, I accept the suggestion of the minister and therefore wish to withdraw the motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
resolution is to be withdrawn on the understanding, I assume, that it is to be referred to the Pension Committee. Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member have leave to withdraw his resolution?
The House gave permission.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.

Speaker of the House of Commons

He said: Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we listened to a very interesting discussion with regard to pensions for widowed mothers of returned soldiers; in fact, since I have had the honour of being a member of this House I have on several occasions had the pleasure of listening to a number of interesting discussions affecting our returned men. For a short time to-night I want to direct the attention of hon. members to our sailors who also fought for their King and country; and although what I am about to discuss will not involve any heavy expenditure, yet I feel, as do a number of our people, that the matter is a very important one.
May I be permitted to say, Sir, that the reason I am asking for these documents is that I received a letter from the Secretary of the Naval Branch of the Great War Veterans' Association of Canada requesting me to take this matter up and obtain the opinion of Parliament regarding the manner in which our sailors have been treated in reference to the service badge issued to those who served either in the Imperial Forces overseas or in the Home Forces in Canadian waters. These sailors are not satisfied with the badge issued to them by the Naval Department of Canada. They feel, Sir, that they should be treated exactly as our soldiers have Been treated in this respect.	[DOT]
The letter to which I have just referred is dated March 2, and is as follows:
The members of this Branch feel very keenly the refusal of the Naval Department to carry out recommendation 14 of the Parliamentary Committee's report. On account of the interest you are taking in naval matters I am instructed to write to you ....
Would it not be possible to have this grievance discussed in the House, especially as a number of naval veterans are being antagonized by the action of the Naval Department.
Now, Mr. Speaker, they say that instead of issuing to the sailors the little bronze badge which we so much admire on the lapels of the coats of our soldiers who fought so gallantly overseas, the Naval Department issued a great big white disc resembling one of the old Mexican dollars, and my information is that these boys are ashamed to wear this badge on their coats.

I may be permitted, Sir, to quote another letter which I have received from a young naval rating who lives in Ashcroft, British Columbia. It is as follows:
I am very pleased indeed to see that you are taking up the matter of the service badge issued to those who served in the Navy during the war. As one of the Naval men who went overseas I wish to state that the badge we have been given is a shame and disgrace and I would not be seen wearing it to a dog fight. As you are probably aware it has much the appearance of some of the military cap badges and in fact is taken for one quite generally. No one ever would dream that it is the service badge issued to its sailors by a grateful country. I trust you will be able to see justice is done the Naval men in this matter.
You will remember, Sir, that last year a committee was appointed by this House to investigate, certain soldier grievances. That committee met a number of times under the chairmanship of the Hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) and at one of those meetings the Great War Veterans' Association made a suggestion with regard to a badge for the naval ratings, which wds adopted by the committee whose report was subsequently submitted to the House, and, if I understand correctly, adopted.
The recommendation to which I refer is contained in the fourteenth clause of the report, and it is in this form:
That members of the Naval Service who have served overseas in either Imperial or Canadian naval services or who have served in any seagoing ship in the Canadian naval service, outside of the three-mile territorial limit, shall be awarded the Class "A" badge with "naval" or suitable words in place of "C.E.F."
Now, Mr. Speaker, in case there is anybody here who does not understand what the Class A badge is, I may say that it is the little bronze badge we see our soldiers wearing on the lapels of their coats. The recommendation was that our naval ratings should be awarded a similar badge, but that instead of the letters "C.E.F." the word "naval" should be engraved thereon.
It is quite evident that this matter is engaging the attention of some of our important newspapers. Under date of March 1, the Toronto Star has an editorial which, with your permission, Sir, I will place on Hansard:

speechtext:
The desire of those Canadians who were in the naval service during the war to be awarded a badge which will be recognizable in this country as denoting that the wearer took part in the war is a perfectly natural one.
The little bronze button worn by the man who fought at the front is a badge of honour, and ever will be. Its significance is known to all
TMr. Duff.]
who see it. Total strangers who wear it, meeting anywhere, establish a bond of understanding at a glance.
The badge which has been issued to the men who saw naval service in the war-and to some who didn't-is a decorative design in silver, too conspicuous for ordinary wear by a modest person. If a man did wear it probably not one person in a hundred in Toronto would know what it meant, and nine out of ten who tried to make a guess as to its meaning would probably regard it as a badge of some sort of noncombatant service. No doubt the tenth person would mistake it for a battalion badge of some sort. The fact is there are not enough naval war service men in the country to introduce this distinctive badge and give it vogue and acceptance.
In the fourth and final report of the Parliamentary Committee on the Re-establishment the 14th suggestion was as follows:
This suggestion I read a moment ago; I shall not repeat it.
It is the carrying out of this recommendation that the returned naval men ask for. In asking this they have the support of the G.W.V.A. organizations here and elsewhere and the editorial support of their organ, The Veteran.
The little bronze badge is the one that counts in Canada

it is the one that every one knows the meaning of and always will, and its meaning is that the wearer risked himself in the Avar and survived such dangers as confronted him in his duties. Already the use of this badge has been extended, and very properly so, to an overseas service not connected with the C.E.F.-those Canadians in the Royal Air Force who flew at the front receiving the badge whether they had formerly been in the military forces or not.
The little bronze badge is the active service war badge of Canada-it is worn by those who saw active service on land and in the air, and should appropriately be extended to those who served on the sea.
I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that the Toronto Star sums the situation up much better than I could. I see no reason why the Naval Department should depart from the recommendation made by the Parliamentary Committee on Soldiers' Civil Be-establishment and issue this distinctive badge to which the naval men object.
Of the Canadians who served, in the Imperial navy during the war, there were about 300 officers and 2,700 men. While these men did not, perhaps, see active service which our soldiers saw in the trenches, they had to face the danger of the submarines, mines, storms, fogs and winds, during the course of their work in the North sea. Any one who knows anything about seafaring life know what conditions these men had to face as day after day and night after night they stood on the decks of small fifty or one-hundred ton boats, keeping watch over the sea and looking after the interests of British people

everywhere. It seems to me that these men are deserving of the distinctive war badge as are the soldiers.
A number of our Canadian boys took part on the dash on Ostend and in the raid on Zeebrugge. We all remember reading with pride of the raid on Zeebrugge, when the English vessels entered the harbour and closed up the gap so that the German submarines could not get out of their bases. .Surely any Canadians who took part in that raid are deserving of the very best that Canada can give them, and when they ask for a war badge similar to that which is given to our gallant soldiers, I see no reason why their request should not be granted.
The Naval Department give some reasons why they have not issued this distinctive metal badge. They say:
1.	" A.A." badge-
That is, the white metal badge.
-fulfils its purpose.
2.	Objections from the military authorities and the military individually.
3.	Naval veterans are satisfied with the white metal badge.
4.	That naval service should not be ranked on a par with military service in the trenches
I am quoting from a letter which was written to me by the Secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association. Perhaps the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Ballan-tyne) will tell us, after I have finished my remarks, whether or not these reasons have been correctly stated.
As to the first objection, I understand that the naval ratings are not satisfied with the white metal badge they would prefer these little bronze badges. The naval ratings say that the white metal badge is not recognized by the public; that it is not suitable to be worn and that " service rendered," the words which appear on the badge, are not adequate or fair.
As to the second objection, that the military authorities and individual soldiers object to the use by the naval ratings of the metal badge, that cannot be correct, because, as I pointed out a few moments ago, at a meeting of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Committee, before which appeared Mr. McNeil, Secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association, and other members of that organization, it was suggested that the same badge be issued to sailors as was being issued to soldiers.
The third reason given is that the naval veterans are satisfied with the white metal badge. Now, Sir, I take exception to that statement; the naval veterans are not satisfied with the white metal badge. I have
on my desk here a number of letters and telegrams which I have received from all over the country since I put this motion on the Order Paper, thanking me for bringing this matter before Parliament and expressing the dissatisfaction of the naval ratings with the white metal badge.
The fourth objection was that the naval service should not be ranked on a par with military service in the trenches. Well, even if that were correct, no naval official should have made the statement. I hope that the minister will be able to say that no such statement was made by the Naval Department, because it seems to me that if our Canadian sailors had been given the chance that they would have been given if we had had Canadian ships on the Canadian coasts, they would have shown their mettle and have done just as good service as was done by the boys in the trenches.
I noticed in the Ottawa Journal a few days ago an announcement which I assume was issued by the Naval Department. It is headed " 1914-15 Bronze Star," and it says:
The Department of the Naval Service announces that the issue of the 1914-15 Bronze Star for service in the Royal Canadian Navy has commenced. The conditions for the award of this decoration are service at sea between August 4, 1914, and December 31, 1915.
I assume from the fact that this badge or star is being issued for service betweeen August, 1914, and December, 1915, that the Naval Department intend to issue a number of badges of different kinds. It .would be far better to issue only one badge. The men do not want these distinctive badges; no reason can be offered for issuing them. I trust that my remarks will be approved by the members of the House and that there will be a general protest to the minister in this matter and a request that only one badge be issued, the same as that which is worn by the soldiers. The cost will surely not be very great. We did not, I am sorry to say, have very many sailors, either in the Imperial or in the Canadian Naval Service; consequently the matter of cost cannot be urged as the reason for the nonissuance of these badges. Even at this late date the department can call in all the white metal badges that have been issued to sailors who served in the naval forces either in Canada or overseas and issue the little bronze badge which is so much admired by everybody. I trust that the minister will listen to the prayer not only of myself, but also of the boys who so gallantly served in our naval forces, and grant their request.
