speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am

grateful to the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) for putting this motion on the Order Paper and also for his warm words of commendation of those who served their country so ably and so gravely in the Eoyal Canadian Naval Service and in the Imperial Navy.
The House may be interested to know that the total number of Canadians who served overseas with the Imperial naval forces was 1,544, and that there were killed in action 26, lost at sea 3; that 11 died of disease and 5 were wounded. All hon. members will look with pride on this showing made by Canadians who served so well in the Imperial Navy during the war. In addition to that, 5,000 men served in the Eoyal Canadian Naval Service on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. The men who served in the senior branch of the service, either in the Imperial Navy or the Canadian Navy, are naturally proud that they have had an opportunity of serving in that branch.
Those who served Overseas shared, of course, in the glorious traditions of the British navy. Those who served in Canada in our own navy must in a lesser degree also have felt proud of being part of the great Imperial navy, which has not only preserved the British Empire to us but has done so much for the peace of the world. I am therefore glad to rise in my place in this House to-night and say on behalf of the 1,144 Canadians who served in the Imperial navy, and on behalf of the very large majority of the 5,000 men who served in our home naval forces, that while they look with pride on their brother Canadians in the Canadian Army corps who Served so bravely on the fields of France and who deserve all the honour and recognition that has come to them, yet they have equal pride in their own force and want a medal that will distinguish the naval service from their brothers-in-arms of the Canadian Army corps. We have therefore issued three classes of badges to the Naval Service of Canada. I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) that a man would not be proud to wear one of these badges. I have a cut of the (badges in my hand. They are of silver, and are very beautifully designed. In order to meet the views of the large number of sailors of all ratings who have served in the Imperial navy and in the Canadian navy for badges that would be distinct from the badges granted to the other branch of the service, after very careful consideration on the part of the Naval Service, by myself as responsible minister, and by the Government, the following, three classes of

badges have been approved by the Government and the Naval Service, and have been issued:
(1)	Naval Class AA. This corresponds to the Militia Class A. This AA badge is issued to those who have served at sea or Overseas and who have been honourably discharged for reasons other than invalided.
(2)	Naval Class A. This corresponds to Militia Class B. The badge is very beautifully designed, and bears the words " For King and Empire. (Services rendered." This badge is similar to the one issued by the Imperial naval authorities.
(3)	Naval Class B. This corresponds to Militia Class C. It is issued to those who have served on shore or in harbour in Canada and have been honourably discharged. It bears the words " For Honourable Services."
I am sure hon. members will agree that we did well to issue badges to honour these brave men who served Canada so well in guarding our own shores.
The hon. member for Lunenburg has suggested that the naval badge might not be known or recognized. I agree. But if my hon. friend had served in the front line trenches I am sure he would be proud to wear the Class A badge issued by the military authorities, and naturally the sailors are proud of the badges that are issued to them. If I had served in the navy, that fine branch of the service, I would not want to wear the badge of the gallant soldiers, much as we admire them; I would want an entirely distinct badge, and would be very proud indeed of the distinction of wearing the Naval Badge AA. If I had been invalided out of the service, nothing would make me feel, more proud than to wear the badge of the invalided men, and if I had only been permitted to serve on shore I would with equal pride want to wear the Naval Badge B.
It is true that there are a few men in the Naval Service who are desirous of wearing the Military Badge A. They would be content to , have the small letters C.E.F. eliminated from the military badge, and equally small letters inserted to make up the word " Naval;" but a naval man walking along the street or going into an office with that badge would at once be taken for an ex-soldier who had served in the front line trenches. Those Canadians who served at sea in the Imperial service and ran all the risks of mines and submarines and the other risks of naval warfare, can feel an equal pride in wearing Class AA badge. It was felt that the man who had served on shore should not receive a badge

of the same class as the man who had served Overseas, and we have therefore followed the practice of the Department of Militia and Defence. That department issues three badges, A, B and C. Badge A is for soldiers who have served in the front line; Badge B for those who have been invalided out of the service; and Badge C foi those who have served at home. Some did not have the privilege of fighting in the front line trenches, but nevertheless they offered their services and did the very best they could. That is true of our men on both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. I am sure my hon. friend appreciates that there were certain dangers even in the patrol service on the Atlantic coast. When the German U-boats came to that coast in the summer of 1918, they strewed the waters with mines, any one of /which these patrol boats might have struck, and at any moment a U-boat might come to the surface; so the men who served in our home forces were exposed to certain risks, particularly on the Pacific coast at the outbreak of the war, and in the later stages of the war on the Atlantic coast.
The hon. member for Lunenburg has referred to a recommendation of the special committee which was appointed last spring to consider Bill No. 10, regarding soldiers' civil re-establishment.
'Suggestion 14, to which the hon. member referred, was as follows:
That the members of the Naval Service who have served overseas in either the Imperial or Canadian Naval 'Services, or who have served in any sea-going 'ship in the Canadian Naval Service, outside of the three-mile territorial limit, shall toe awarded a Class "A" toadge with "Naval1' or suitable words in place of "C.E.P."
This was the suggestion that was made to the special parliamentary committee, and the following is their recommendation, which the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) omitted to give us, possibly not having it in his possession:
It is recommended that the suggestion should receive the immediate attention of the Government with a view to removing a cause of complaint which, in the opinion of the committee, appears to he well-founded. The same may be also true of the R.A.P. If so, the matter should receive the attention of the Government.
There is nothing in this paragraph in the nature of any definite suggestion to the Government; it merely brings the matter to their attention. The 'Government gave due consideration to the recommendations of the parliamentary committee, and having done so decided to issue the badges which I have fully described to the House.
The hon. member for Lunenburg referred to the Royal Air Force badge being the same as the soldiers' badge, and I think it is buit fit and proper that the two should be the same. The Royal Air Force is part of the army. It is not under the Admiralty, but under the control and direction of the Commander-in-Chief of the British Army, Sir Douglas Haig; and when the badges were being given to men of the Royal Air Force they would naturally be the same as those given to the soldiers in the army.
With regard to the medals that have been mentioned, I may say that the Admiralty will give medals, which I shall describe in a moment, to all ratings in the British Navy, and I think that our Canadian men have a right to be given the same medals. These medals are: 1914-15 Star: Service at sea between August 4, 1914, and December 31, 1915; British War Medal (General Service Medal), for those who have been 28 days mobilized in the service; Victory Medal, for those who have served at sea between August 4, 1914, and November 11, 1918. I shall make it my duty, and indeed it will be a pleasure to me, to see that these medals are given to all Canadian naval ratings, both those that were in the Imperial service a!nd those that served at home.
Are the badges mentioned by the hon. minister to be given to men in the British navy or to Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To men in the British navy. I shall not take up any more time on the subject, but I desire to say that if we granted a badge similar in design to that issued to the Canadian soldiers it would not satisfy the majority of the thousands of our men who served either overseas or in our Canadian naval service. It would also antagonize the Great War Veterans, and I do not think the Militia Council would approve Of it. On the whole, I think that any fair-minded man who has served in either the naval or the military forces will recognize ithe need of having distinctive badges for the two services; and I hope, in view of the brief explanation which I have given to the House this evening, that the hon. member may see his way clear to withdraw his motion.

I am interested in this matter because of representations made by large numbers of the naval veterans in Toronto-hundreds of them-that they feel keenly their treatment, which they regard as being unfair. The minister has said about everything that

could be said in defence of his part in this matter, and has said it extremely well, as he always does. But at the same time he seems to me to fall short of explaining something that needs explanation, namely, that the report of the committee-the largest and most important that has sat in this House for years, a committee that sat day in and day out, week after week- came to a conclusion different from the opinions which have just been expressed. The point I wish to call to the attention of the House is that it is not the minister who took this position, but two of his officials. The report of the committee was adopted by this House on the 7th of November last year, but we find that on the 31st of October, -a week before, one of the officials of the Naval Service Department took it on himself to say that we should not have that badge which rwas recommended by the parliamentary committee, of course, that was going pretty far.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me, I should like to correct his statement that my officials decided the question. The whole matter was decided by myself as the head of the department, and if there is any blame to be attributed to any one I am the responsible person.

That is very generous ot my hon. friend, but it is incumbent upon me to point to the date of the letter of Admiral Kingsmill regarding the matter, and I venture to say that the minister will admit the truth of my contention.
Do I understand the hon. member to say that the report to which he has referred was adopted? If I remember rightly it was only received.

I understood that the report of the committee on the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was adopted and passed on the 7th of November. Whether that is so or not, however, it was received and virtually adopted by a large majority of the House. The letter to which I refer is dated October 31st, and I may read from it:
There appears to be no reason why the badges issued for naval service should not be recognized in the same way as those issued for military service except that, as there are comparatively few naval men in Canada, the public have not become familiar with the naval badges or the service which they denote, though a description of the badges and regulations governing their issue have been published in the press; and there is no doubt that in some cases discharged naval men have suffered injustice through the public not understanding the significance of the badges awarded to them.

The letter does not refer in any way to the fact, which wad afterwards discovered, that there were some objections from the Department of Militia.
But that comes a couple of months later in a letter from the Deputy Minister of Naval Service. What happened was this: The admiral and the deputy minister came to the conclusion that they will make a badge, and they design a silver badge which the men do not like. But it would seem to be lese majeste to suggest that the badge designed by these two officials was not the thing for the soldiers and sailors, and the minister apparently thinks it would be a good thing to have some advice from the Department of Militia and Defence. He says:
It was considered necessary that the opinion of the Militia Department be obtained before taking any action.
Although we had declared in this House that this particular badge with the word "Naval" should be issued to the sailors. He says further:
There appears to be no reason why these badges should not receive due recognition.
The Naval Department, therefore does not feel justified in issuing a badge similar to the Class "A" Militia. Badge, when by so doing it is clear that great dissatisfaction would be caused.
There is no evidence of dissatisfaction. As a matter of fact, the secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association, Mr. Mae-Neil, was present at the committee; he is a soldier, he represents the soldiers; there were all sorts of officials present; and it was stated that the sailors asked for this particular badge. Any objection which came from the Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs or from the Militia Department afterwards must have come with very poor grace after the matter had been decided by the committee. How was _this badge issued by the committee and how did they come to the conclusion that it would be better to make no distinction, or very little distinction, between the badges to be worn by the soldiers and the sailors? They are both fighting the battle of the country; they are both looking for jobs when they come back. When the men get back and line up before an em-jloyer in order to get a job, it is a great advantage to a returned man to have a service badge. But if he wears a silver badge which nobody knows anything about, and which, although it may be very dear to the heart of the officials of the Naval Service, is not relished at all by the sailors themselves, and which may look like a badge of the Ancient Order of Pelicans, or something of that kind, he is not likely to be selected by

the employer. That was said by a gentleman who appeared before the committee, a gentleman who entered the service as a sailor and afterwards rose to the rank of a petty officer. Here is what he says:
Q. What is the point there?-A. Canadian sailors, I think, are the Canadians that have served overseas on active service that are not being granted the recognized active service button. This places all classes of sailors at a disadvantage.
Q. In the public estimation?-A. In the public estimation, a returned sailor going in to see an employer asking for a position, there is probably a line-up of men asking for employment and the employer does not stop to ask questions, his eye instinctively travels to the left lapel of the man's coat to see if the button is there and if the man is a strong, vigorous, active young man fit for service the employer simply asks no questions, but suggests that he go somewhere else to look for a position.
That is the evidence of the secretary of the Naval Branch, who was promoted during the war. I have also the evidence of an officer of the force and which shows that our sailors went all over the world. I refer to Captain A. C. Turner, whose evidence will be found at page 927: He says:
If I may take my own case as an example, I first of all went to England and was kept there a few months. Then I was sent to Gallipoli and the Dardanelles. Prom there I was sent back to the Channel and I had comand of my own ship in the attacks on Zeebrugge and Os-tend. From there I went to the north of Scotland. For that service I have nothing to show. Until six months after the armistice there was no button that we could wear to show that we had been overseas. Lately the Naval Service Department issued a large white metal badge which however entirely failed in its purpose. First of all, it is not known to the public, and therefore is of no value. The only button of any value, so far as the public is concerned is that for service at the front. Secondly, that button in its wording is absolutely inadequate. It simply says, " For service rendered." It does not indicate the service. That is our request about the badge and our members feel very strongly about it. It puts them in an unfair position both in business and in private life. They fail to see why a line should be drawn between them and the men who went overseas as soldiers. Most of these three hundred Canadian Naval officers did exceptionally good work in various parts of the world. They went because they knew more about naval matters than about infantry or gunner work or military matters. They thought they could serve their country best in that way, and yet until about two months ago they had been given no badge of any description.
Q. Did you say you were at Zeebrugge?-A. Yes, I had the honour of being in command of a motor launch at Zeebrugge and I was later at the successful action against Ostend. ,
Q. You were under fire?-A. We were under fire for two hours and forty minutes at Zeebrugge and for two hours at Ostend. You have probably heard Captain Carpenter speak of that action.	All who were
in it were right in shore.	Up to six or
eight weeks ago there was not a button or a badge of any description that I could secure or that any Canadian Naval officers could secure to show that we had seen service. Now we have got a badge that is equal to the Class B badge. It is too large to be worn on the lapel of the coat, and it is absolutely unknown to the general public.
Q. Did you make application to the Admiralty or to the Canadian authorities for a badge? -A. We did, and that is the result.
Q. What sort of badge is it that you desire? -A. We desire one for service at the front; perhaps instead of the words " C.E.F." some suitable word such as " Naval " or " Naval Service."
That evidence so impressed the committee, sitting there deliberating and hearing the whole thing, that they came to the conclusion that is found in the report. I do not think that the report should be whittled down to the fine point to which it has been whittled by the minister because I am quite sure that it was meant by this House to give these sailors what they asked for. It is recommended that:
The suggestion should receive the immediate attention of the Government with a view to removing a cause of complaint which, in the opinion of the committee, appears to be well founded. The same may be also true of the R.A.F.
It appears that the R.A.F. had a Naval Service button known to all as the R.A.F. button. But when it comes down to interfering with this little silver badge that nobody wants but the officials of the Naval Service there is all the difference in the world. They make no difference between a man on the ground and a man in the air but they make a tremendous difference between a man on the ground and a man on the sea. There is nothing to warrant this. While I respectfully beg to commend the minister for the way in which he has defended the department I do not think they have done the just thing by these men. The minister says:	I would not want to
wear that little badge. The minister has not been overseas but those who have been overseas do want to wear this well known badge. They say it helps them in civil life, and I do not think that the minister or anybody else should now say:	It is my
duty to decide what they want, or what they think they want. It is rather the duty of the minister to give them what they do want. I think it would be a very small thing to scrap this silver badge, issue a war badge, and give that badge to all returned soldiers and sailors.

Mr. Speaker while there may be something to be said in support of the view advanced by

the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) the fact remains that we have two arms of the service; the senior arm-the navy, and the other arm-the army. The Naval Department have issued two badges for the navy. The army have also issued their badges. There seems to be nothing improper in that, no differentiation against the Naval Service. In fact, as I said before, they are the senior arm of the service, and should have the badge which belongs to that arm. Given that, everything is being done for them that could he done and possibly in that respect they have an advantage over the army. To any one who has thought enough of the navy to enter it, as compared with entering the army-surely the love of such men for that particular branch of our forces will still continue, and they ought to desire a distinctive badge for that service. It does not seem to me that any practical difficulty could he encountered in the wearing of that badge. Any man wearing it ought to be pleased to explain to any Canadian who had not sufficient knowledge of our affairs to recognize the badge, that it was a badge of the Canadian Navy. The members of that service are connected with the great British Navy which after all, in the British Empire, always has been, and possibly always will be, more important than our army. The traditions and associations of the British Navy are theirs, and they surely will be glad to have a badge which is peculiarly connected with those traditions and associations. Then we must look to the future in a country like Canada. With our vast coast line on three oceans Canada must have naval protection in some form or other. In the future we must have a navy along our coasts, and if that be the case there is no better way of educating our people to the fact that we have a navy, that we have men who fight for us in that navy, than that those men shall wear ,a distinctive naval badge.
Reference has been made to the report of the committee and it recommended that some button should be given. The committee did go so far as to say that the complaints in regard to the matter appeared to be well founded and that the question should be considered by the minister. That inquiry, however, was only a side line in the investigation, the main subject was that of the extent of the gratuity or direct help that should be given to our soldiers. The hon. member (Mr. Mowat) has mentioned the case of the Royal Air Force and the minister explained that that was a part of the army. We might also say that the

Royal Naval Air Force is a part of the navy, and doubtless in the future will be classified under it.
I do not think any one in Canada will feel dissatisfied in that the men of the Naval Service hold a naval decoration rather than an army decoration. I would not go so far as to say that the men who have served in the army would have no objection to the naval men wearing this badge. I think that all these men have the highest regard for naval men, but the soldiers' idea of discipline and orderliness would tend to make them think that as a general principle it will be more in accord with army and navy practice that each branch of the service should have their own peculiar and distinct decoration.

I would not enter into this debate had I not had the experience the other day of seeing one of these badges and therefore can well understand the disinclination of the naval men to wearing it. If you have ever, Mr. Speaker, seen the Highlander in full regalia you surely would have noticed the badge or broach on his left shoulder fastening his shawl. Now the badge in question is almost as large as the brooch you see on members of the Highland Brigade. It may be that the minister, who no doubt looks well in the regalia of a Scottish regiment, was duly impressed with the idea of the traditional Highland costume.
The trouble with the minister in this matter is that he does not understand the mentality of the sailor, although he is at the head of the navy, and for a long time was a harbour commissioner of the harbour of Montreal. The sailor, Mr. Speaker, is a brave and a modest man; his bravery is only equalled by his modesty. This medal or badge is one which on an ordinary lapel will extend over each side for at least one-eighth of an inch and is of bright, shiny metal. I do not think it is silver, because silver is so valuable these days, that the Minister of Finance would scarcely allow the Department of Naval Service to issue such a badge in real silver. It is more likely a mixture of tin and zinc, a-bright shiny, white metal. The fact of the matter is that we should give our sailors, who are just as much entitled to credit for their bravery as our soldiers, no more and no less than the latter. We should give them a badge that they would be pleased to wear and not a badge that is so conspicuous that it offends a man's sense of modesty to wear it. I speak with perfect seriousness in this matter. We should give our sailors a badge which is as attractive as that of the army but

sufficiently different to be distinguishable from it. It should be of such a size and so inconspicuous that a modest man would be pleased to wear it. Hundreds of thousands of young men all over the country are wearing army service buttons, but I see very few men wearing the brooch-for it is a sort of a brooch-which the Department of Naval Service has issued. I believe the reason for that is that men do not like to make themselves unduly conspicuous.
1 would urge upon the House the wisdom of the motion made by the hon. member (Mr. Duff). I do not often find myself in complete agreement with the words of the member for Parkdale, but the fact that I do find myself in complete agreement with what he said to-night will, I trust, add weight to his words.
Mr. E, W. NESBITT (North Oxford): 1 would like to endorse what my hon. friend for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) has said. So far as the conclusions of the committee were concerned the whole of their report was a recommendation to the House, and that .part of the report dealing with this particular matter was just as much a recommendation as the other matters treated in the report. The reason why the committee came to the conclusion it did was because it was waited on by various members of the Naval Brigade; and when the young fellow who commanded a motor boat at Zeebrugge -probably one of the most daring feats ever carried out by the British navy-when he applied personally to have the badge changed and to have a badge similar to the organizations that have been mentioned, I had no hesitation in supporting the suggestion to change the badge, and that these young men should be given the type they wanted. As the hon. member for Parkdale asked, what difference does it make to us? These young men only want what they certainly have earned, and as the cost will not be very great the committee could not see any reason why the request should not be granted.

Mr. Speaker, I ' did not intend to take any part in this discussion until I heard the speech of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). After listening to him I concluded that he was trying to camouflage himself to the world as a Highlander!
I come of decent Lowland folk and never did anything of the kind.

The name " McMaster " has graced the personnel of many a Highland regiment. But, like Peter of old, his language has betrayed him to-night, and he shocked my modesty very much by asking: What sort of a shawl this is that a Highlander wears? Let me tell my hon. friend from Brome that that is the shawl which was worn by the 42nd Highlanders at the Battle of Waterloo; that the same shawl was worn by the Highlanders at the Relief of Lucknow; and that the same shawl was worn by Highlanders in the many battles all over the world where they have distinguished themselves and brought honour and glory to their King and country.
The pin or brooch which my hon. friend knows so little about is the clasp with which the Highlander fastens his plaid across his broad shoulders,-and if the badge which has been issued to these sailors bears any resemblance to the Highlander's brooch, I have no sympathy with any man refusing to wear it.
I did not hear the speech of my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) which I regret very much, and I heard only part of the speech of the Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Ballantyne), but I thought it was worth while, for the education and edification of my hon. friend from Brome, that I should give him some information about the shawl and the brooch and the reason for the pride with which Highlanders wear their plaid and every other part of their

uniform from the bonnet to the buckle on their shoes.
I can quite understand, Mr. Speaker, that there should be some distinction between the badges awarded to the several classes of our Canadian forces. There is nothing too honourable to be worn by our soldiers who were at the front or who tried to get there; and there is equal distinction coming to any man who honourably served his country in the Naval Service where real service was performed. But I am not in sympathy with giving any decoration to men who during the war served in what was called the Canadian Navy, because I submit, Mr. Speaker, that so far as I know -and I know a good deal about them- they did not do very much that entitled them to any honour. I do not think they were serving with the idea of being awarded medals. At any rate, they had no opportunity of distinguishing themselves because they had not any fighting ships, and certainly it would not be fair to put a man who served in our Canadian Navy upon the same footing as the man who served in the British Navy during the war. If badges are to be issued for naval men I hope a distinction will be made and that it will be given to our men who served in the British Navy rather than to those who were engaged around our own coast in absolute security and who *were able to return to harbour every night and sleep soundly in their beds. Possibly if I had heard the whole speech of the hon. minister I would have no doubt as to the different classes of badges that are to be issued. But I would join my voice with those who say that these naval men should be given the kind of badge they require so long as it does not interfere with the distinctive badge issued to the soldiers.

Mr. Speaker, on 7th of November, 1919, the report that I referred to was adopted by this House. On that date, I see, a division was taken and the main motion that the report of the committee be received was agreed to. So the member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is wrong. Of course, as this is not a private fight anybody can get into it, but I have not taken sides in ithe matter because 1 do not understand the question. The point, however, is, that since this report was agreed to by the House it certainly shuts out all criticism of it; it would be an entirely different thing were it only received,-especially in view of the fact that the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has come down so heavily and

almightily on the whole situation as to say that it was not adopted but only received.
That is a pure technicality. It does not matter.
Mr. Speaker, I-

Mr. Speaker, I will not take up much time replying to the arguments put forward by the hon. Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Rallantyne). It seems to me that after what has been said by hon. members who support me in this matter there is only one thing for the minister to do-to recall the badges already issued and to issue the badge which the sailors require.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you noticed that during the minister's remarks he did not tell us whether the sailors asked for those particular badges which he has been issuing. I would like to know who did ask for them. Was it the sailors, or, as the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) suggests, did the request come from the officials of the department?
We know that the minister is large-hearted. Last year, Sir, when I made a speech with reference to the Canadian navy, he was so big-hearted that he wanted to take on his shoulders not only the sins of the officials of his department while he was minister, but their sins while under his predecessor. To-night he is doing the very same thing, he is shouldering the sins of his officials who were responsible for these monstrosities.
The minister did me the honour of sending me a few minutes 'ago specimens of the three different badges which he has issued. The first one, as I have already said, is a monstrosity. It is certainly no honour to the scarf-pin which the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. D. D. McKenzie) and I wear when we don our kilts. Further, Sir, I say it is an insult on the part of the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to refer to this monstrosity as something like the scarf-pin which Scotchmen wear.
This first badge, Sir, consists of two fouled anchors. That will enable the House to form an estimate of the artistic capabilities of the designer. You know, when a vessel gets her anchor fouled she goes adrift. Well, I suppose

that is what is going to happen to these sailors. God knows that they had opportunity enough of going adrift while they were at sea; the minister evidently intends now to send them adrift with a heavy disc on their left lapels. Above these two fouled anchors there is a scroll; then a great, big crown. Sir, the thing is not fit to wear; I would not have my dog wear it, let alone give it to a man who has served in the naval forces.
Now, I was not a sailor during the war, nor was I a soldier, but the member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) said, as I understood him, that the army was the senior arm of the service.
He said, .the navy.

Then I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; I thought he said that the army was the senior arm. I contend that the British navy is the senior arm of our forces. I say, then, that if the Great War Veterans' Association is satisfied that the same badge be issued to sailors as is issued to soldiers, all members of Parliament, the minister included, should agree that the one badge be issued.
Somebody has evidently told the minister that the Great War Veterans' Association objected to the use by sailors of this metal badge. The secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association, Mr. McNeil, assures me that the executive of the Dominion Command of that association is unanimously in favour of the recommendation to which I refer. Whether it was adopted, makes no difference; the fact is that the committee brought down this recommendation to the House; a recommendation which was endorsed by the military branch of the Great War Veterans' Association, as well as the Ontario Command. If the soldiers are willing that their comrades in the navy wear a badge the same as that worn by them, with the substitution of "Navy" for " C.E.F.," then the minister should scrap the different badges which he is issuing and issue a bronze badge similar to that which the soldiers are wearing.
The minister said that he was following the example of the British navy. Well, the British navy is a very old institution, and I can understand why they find it necessary to have distinctive badges or medals. But the Canadian navy comprises a very small part of the forces which we sent overseas; consequently it is not necessary for us to have three or four distinctive badges. As I have said, my only idea in bringing this matter up is to comply with the request of the Great War Veterans' Association and also of a number of sailors from whom I have received letters and telegrams. Under the circumstances the minister should, I think, reconsider this matter, and issue the same badge for sailors as is issued for soldiers.

Minister's Office,
Ottawa, September 22, 1919.
My dear Sir Robert Borden,-In the reorganization of the Cabinet, which you now have under consideration, I trust you will not

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
overlook the request I made to you some little time ago, to permit me to retire from my present position In the Government.
As I stated to you then, I accepted the portfolio of Minister of Militia and Defence ('Canada) with a keen desire to play my part in assisting you in every way possible to bring the war to a successful conclusion, and to support the Canadian Corps at the front with reinforcements. On the termination of the war, and before you left for the Peace Conference, at your request, I agreed to stay on for a time to carry out, so far as this department was concerned, the big problem of demobilization. As this task is just about completed, and as this department will now be reorganized on a peace basis, I feel that ray contract has terminated and that the administration of the department should now be handed over to some one else.
While the war was on I did not hesitate to sacrifice everything I had to give my service to my country, I have been absent from my home and my ' business for nearly five years, and have been compelled to neglect my practice and my private affairs, but I feel repaid, inasmuch as I have had the privilege of doing something to support you, in a small way, in the enormous responsibilities that have been cast upon your shoulders since the 4th of August, 191.4. During this long period, in the various offices I have been privileged to occupy in the public service, I have endeavoured to the best of my ability to conscientiously carry out my duties faithfully and to give you my very best support.
X feel that the time has come when I must, in fairness to my family, take a short rest and give personal attention to my private affairs that have been sadly neglected for so long. I would, therefore, ask you to accept my resignation as Minister of Militia and Defence at the earliest possible date.
I wish to express to you my very deep appreciation of the confidence you have reposed in me, and of the very loyal1 and whole-hearted support you have given to me while I have been a member of your Cabinet, and. I trust that confidence will continue for all time.
I have the honour to 'be, tny dear Sir Robert Tour obedient servant,
S. C. Mewburn.

Sir Robert Borden, P.C., G.CM.G.,
