Resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed resolution of Mr. Burnham:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that to the extent of the jurisdiction of ithis Parliament a national eight-hour working day should be established immediately, subject only to the right of express private contract.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on this resolution from the point of view of the farmer. If this resolution carries and the eight-hour day becomes law in Canada, I do not see how we shall be able to carry it out on the farm. There is a great deal of lost time on the farm on account of inclement weather. To-day we are paying higher salaries than were ever paid in Canada for farm labour; in my own district we are paying from $75 to $100 a month. During the greater part of the summer, during seeding and the summer fallow, we must work our teams at least nine hours a day in order to get our work done. If we do that we are in the position of having to pay a man time and a half for overtime or of hiring a stableman to take care of the teams when they come from the farm and to get them ready to go out to work the next morning. Then, during harvest time when the grain is ripe and hundreds of acres are standing ready to cut, we must work ten or twelve hours a day to get the cutting done. I do not know how 'many hours they work in Ontario during threshing time, but I know that our machines start at daylight and work until dark, and sometimes after.
When our teams are hauling grain to the elevators it is often eight or nine o'clock before they get back to the farm. If the eight-hour day goes into effect in Canada it will simply mean that living, instead of becoming cheaper, will become dearer in this country. It will mean an increase of fifty per cent in the price of farm products. We have no objection to an eight-hour day in shops and factories. They can work eight or ten hours a day if they wish, but I do not see why we should pass legislation in this House to restrict the working hours of
29.
possibly the only people in Canada who seem to be willing to work-the farmers. I shall be compelled to vote against the motion.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council: Mr. Speaker, the question which is raised by this motion was one that engaged the attention of the Washington Conference, and as what was done at that conference may have some bearing upon this matter I think it is only right to put the House in possession of the facts. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is here, he can speak to the House on the constitutional aspect of the case.
Hon. members will recall that under the labour clauses of the Treaty of Peace, it is declared that among the conditions of labour which are producing "unrest so great that the peace and harmony of the world are imperilled " are the hours of labour, and among the measures which it is recommended should be adopted is one " regulating the hours of work, including the establishment of a maximum working day and week." Among the principles laid down in the treaty as of urgent importance is: "The adoption of an eight-hour day or a forty-eight-hour week as the standard to be aimed at where it has not been already attained." And in the agenda for the Washington Conference as set out in the Treaty the first article is " the application of the principle of the eight-hour day and the forty-eight-hour week."
I have referred to these matters in order to indicate to the House the exact nature of the question that came before the Washington Conference for consideration. The question before the Conference was not whether it was desirable or undesirable to pass legislation regulating the hours of labour. That principle was affirmed in the Treaty of Peace; and in all the provinces of the Dominion legislation has been passed regulating the hours of labour in certain classes of industry and among particular classes of workers, particularly women and children. So that principle is recognized in the legislation of Canada and, I think, of all civilized countries. Nor was it the question of whether, in regulating the hours of labour an eight-hour day or a forty-eight hour week would be wise or unwise. That general principle was also laid down in the Treaty. The question which the Washington Conference was called upon to consider was whether there should be an eight-hour day or a forty-eight-hour week or some modification or combination of the two, and whether the



time had arrived to secure general application of that principle to all industrial nations. Hon. members of the House will recognize that one of the principles underlying the labour clauses of the Peace Treaty is that uniform action should be secured on these matters among the industrial nations, that the failure of one or more industrial nations to take action on any of these matters embarrassed, and, in a measure prevented other nations from taking advanced ground. Therefore the issue before the Conference was to ascertain if an agreement could be secured among the representatives of the nations members of the Conference whereby these nations would move forward together in a matter of this kind. What action did the Washington Conference take on this matter and how is such action to be made effective? I will tell the House briefly for the information of hon. gentlemen. Article 19 of the labour clauses provides:
When the Conference has decided on the adoption of proposals with regard to an item in the agenda, dt will rest with the Conference to determine whether these proposals should take the form; (a) of a recommendation to be submitted to the members for consideration with a view to effect being given to it by national legislation or otherwise, or (b) of a draft international convention for ratification by the members.
Hon. members will see that it was open to the Conference to adopt either of these two courses, either to set forth its conclusions in the form recommended which would go forward to the different nations with the view to unite giving effect thereto by national, or the Conference might decide that its decision should take the form of an international treaty or convention to be signed and ratified by the nations parties to the Conference if they approved,
This same article also provides the vote necessary to make .the decision effective :
A majority of two-thirds of the votes cast by the delegates present shall be necessary on the final vote for the adoption of the recommendation or draft convention, as the case may be, by the Conference.
In the case of this particular convention the necessary two-third majority was secured. Now what follows when a convention is adopted? That is also provided in Article 19;
A copy of the recommendation or draft convention shall be authenticated by the signature of the president of the Cpnference and of the Director, and shall be deposited with the Secretary-General of the League of Nations. The Secretary-General will communicate a certified copy of the recommendation or draft convention to each of the members.
[Mr. Rowell. 1
Now by reason of the fact that the Washington Conference was held prior to the League of Nations being constituted, because the ratification of the Treaty did not become effective till the 10th of January, the Conference was not formally closed, but was adjourned until after the Treaty of Peace had gone into effect by reason of its ratification, and the Conference was formally closed by declaration of the governing body at the meeting held in Paris after the Treaty had gone into effect. Before action is taken a certified copy of this .convention must be sent to the secretary of the League of Nations, and a certified copy must be sent by him to each member. The Government has not yet received the certified copy of this or of any of the conventions adopted by the International Labour Conference at Washington.
Therefore the Government is not in receipt of any official communication up to the present time upon which it can take official action. This clause also sets out the obligation which shall rest upon 'each member.
Each of the members undertakes that it will, within the period of one year at most from the closing of the session of the Conference, or, if it is impossible owing to exceptional circumstances to do so within the period of one year, then at the earliest practicable moment, and in no case later than eighteen months from the closing of the session of the Conference, bring the recommendation or draft convention before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies for the enactment of legislation or other action.
The members of the House will see that that raises an important question, particularly in a country like Canada, with a federal constitution, as to whether the legislative authority before which this matter should be brought for appropriate action would be the legislatures of the provinces or the federal parliament. It goes on:
In the case of a draft convention, the member will, if it obtains the consent of the authority or authorities wiithin whose competence the matter lies, communicate the formal ratification of the convention to the Secretary-General and will take such action as may be necessary to make effective the provisions of such convention.
Then there is a further express provision dealing with a federal state:
In the case of a federal state, the power of which to enter into conventions on labour matters is subject to limitations, it shall be in the discretion of that government to treat a draft convention to which such limitations apply as a recommendation only, and the provisions of this article with respect to recommendations shall apply in such case.

As the Minister of Justice is here I shall not undertake to discuss the constitutional aspect of the question either in relation to the federal parliament, or the rights and powers of the provincial legislatures.
I cannot hear what the minister is saying, but I should like to know whether it is his opinion that this Parliament has no jurisdiction in the matter at all.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What I said was that, as the Minister of Justice was here, and as he has been giving the whole matter serious consideration, I would not undertake to pass upon that aspect of it. The Minister of Justice will be able to state the position as he sees it.
Will the Minister of Justice make a statement on that particular question before this debate is over?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I desire to ask a question of the minister (Mr. Rowell) in order that we may fully understand the procedure. In the event of this draft convention being submitted to a parliament that has jurisdiction and such parliament deciding not to take the action suggested in the convention, what would be the consequence of its position?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot undertake at
this moment to answer the question raised by my hon. friend. He will see that it involves a very important question, under our constitution, which would require very careful consideration. My hon. friend no doubt understands that the obligation of a government to submit a convention is exactly the same whether or not that government agrees with the principle of the convention. It may be open to very serious argument that a government, under our system, in submitting such a recommendation, should Submit it so as to permit a free and open vote of the members of the House. That is one view of the matter. The other view would be that the government must take the responsibility of submitting the convention to the House as a government. But it would be a rather anomalous and embarrassing situation if the government were bound to submit to parliament a convention against which it had voted at the conference and with the principle of which it did not agree, and to put it forward as a government measure, virtually saying that parliament must adopt it. I mention this merely to indicate that, here again is a very 29i
important question which will require the most careful consideration before a precedent is established which might to some extent bind subsequent governments. The matter is not free from very serious difficulty in the consideration of its constitutional aspect.
May I ask when steps will be taken to settle the question of jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That whole question is
now under the consideration of the Department of Justice. This afternoon I promised my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) at his request that I would make a statement to the House in regard to the terms of the Washington Convention, so that hon. members might be informed on the subject; and in view of this, and the fact that the Minister of Justice will make a statement in reference to the question of jurisdiction, I would ask my hon. friend to withdraw the motion, because he has accomplished his purpose in bringing the subject to the attention of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In order that we may clearly understand the powers of governments in this matter, will my hon. friend explain to the House how any government will be made to carry out any convention that is agreed upon? As I understand the minister, there is an international convention drafted, and it is submitted to the governments of the different countries that are members of the League of Nations. Should any one of those nations decide not to carry out the convention, by what means will it be coerced, or is there any means of doing this?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I explained the other afternoon in discussing the Bulgarian Treaty, there is no means of compelling a government to carry out any convention. The obligation of the Government is to present the matter to -the competent legislative authority, for consideration and action. If that body determine that the convention shall not be accepted, or, in the case of a recommendation, that it shall not be acted upon, then the government has discharged its whole responsibility under the terms of the Treaty. But there is a provision requiring the government to submit the convention to the competent authority, and any government declining to do so might be subject to an economic boycott and the other penalties provided for to insure the enforcement of the provisions of the treaty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is the
point which I desired to bring out. I wanted to know the method by which obligations were to be enforced.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It depends, in the last
analysis, upon the public opinion of any country, as voiced through its competent legislative assembly, whether any convention shall or shall not be accepted in that particular country.

Suppose this Parliament were found to have no jurisdiction, the jurisdiction being in the provincial legislatures, what would be the position of the Dominion then in relation to the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In that event, the whole responsibility of the Government of Canada would be to submit the matter to the respective provinces, and it would he for the provinces to decide what action they should take. The whole obligation of this Government would be discharged if it submitted the matter to the provinces.
Have the provinces any status in connection with the League of Nations and how do they come into juxtaposition?	'

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The treaty expressly provides for, and contemplates, the case of states with a federal constitution. The matter came up in considering the position of the United States. Brazil also has a federal constitution and provision was made in the treaty for such cases. The reason the treaty says, "Competent legislative authority" is that it was considered that some of these matters might come within the competence of provincial parliaments and not within the competence of the Federal Parliament.

Do I understand the
President of the Privy Council to say that if the Department of Justice, or the highest judicial authority of the land, decides that this matter is within the purview of the provincial legislatures, and one of the provincial governments refuses to submit the agreement to the legislative body, or the legislature refuses to take it into consideration, a boycott will be resorted to? Are the other provinces of the Dominion to refuse to do business with this particular province -to boycott it?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has misunderstood what I said. I said nothing of that kind. What I said was that in cases where jurisdiction rests in the provinces 
and not in the Dominion, the whole obligation is discharged when the Federal Government passes on the recommendation to the province. There is no boycott, the provinces are not obligated to take action and the Federal Parliament has no authority to compel them to take action. The only case where the obligations of the treaty could be brought into play would be if the Federal Government declined to take any action or declined to submit the convention or recommendation to the competent legislative authority.
The way out is for the Federal Government to deny its jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It cannot deny it if it has it. But the Minister of Justice will discuss these matters of jurisdiction, and I think we will save time by leaving them to him to discuss.
Has my hon. friend in mind the date of the Washington conference?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: November.
I understand that the official report has not yet been received by the Government of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The conference,' as I explained, only adjourned; it did not conclude its session. The reason it did not conclude its session was because, owing to the delay in the ratification of the Treaty of Peace, the treaty had not been ratified when the conference concluded its regular business. Therefore the conference formally adjourned, instead of closing its session, and the conference was proclaimed closed some time in the month of January or February -I do not remember the date-by action in Paris, when the executive, or governing body, met. The chairman and secretary of the conference could not transmit any convention to the secretary of the League of Nations prior to the formal closing of the conference, and the secretary-general of the League of Nations could not transmit certified copies to the nations which are members of the League of Nations until he had received them from the chairman of the conference. Therefore, all have not received them. But there has been no great delay in dealing with the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether, in his opinion, the circumstance of the United States not having become a member of the League of Nations would have any effect in delaying a con-

elusion upon the question as to whether the Federal Government ought to take action on this convention.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would be an important factor to be taken into consideration. Now,, just a word or two as to what the convention does provide. In the first place, it differs from the resolution before the House in that the resolution provides for a general eight-hour day irrespective of the classes Of occupations. The convention recognizes that there are three or four groups, of employees and it divides them into industry, agriculture, commerce, and those who go to sea. The convention only covers industry. It does not cover agriculture, commerce, or seamen. Thus it is narrowed down to employees engaged in industry.
May I ask the hon. gentleman to explain the difference between industry and agriculture?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The distinction is drawn in the treaty in this way: The treaty sets out certain classes of employment which shall be called "industrial undertakings." It provides:
For the purposes of this Convention the term "industrial undertaking:" includes particularly :
(o) Mines, quarries, and other works for the extraction of minerals from the earth.
(b) Industries in which articles are manufactured, altered, cleaned, repaired, ornamented, finished, adapted for sale, broken up or demolished, or in which materials are transformed ; including shipbuilding and the generation, transformation and transmission of electricity or motive power of any kind.
It goes on to define certain other specified undertakings which are classed as industry, including works of construction, building railways, transport of passengers or goods by sea or land. Then it adds-and this meets the point which my hon. friend has raised-
The competent authority in each country shall define the line of division which separates industry and commerce from agriculture.
It is referred to the competent legislative authorities in each country to, draw the line between industry, agriculture and commerce.

' Does not the first clause include agriculture? It says:	"other
means of producing or extracting things from the earth."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, agriculture is expressly excluded and is referred to the competent authority in each country to draw the line

Agriculture is
chiefly concerned with transforming materials into something a little different. It is not merely a matter of sowing the seed and reaping the harvest.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend evidently did not catch what I said. It is extracting minerals from the earth; not materials from the earth.
Materials transformed.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend can see the document and peruse it for himself. It makes it quite clear that it does not apply to agriculture. There is no mistake; it is made clear beyond peradventure. The Convention provides for an eight-hours day and a forty-eight hours week, subject to the exception set forth in the Convention. These exceptions are briefly as follows: (1) Persons holding positions of superintendence or management or employed in a confidential capacity; (2) where the hours of work on one or more days of the week are fewer than eight, the limit of eight hours may be exceeded by not more than one hour per day. Where there is a Saturday half holiday then the other days of the week may exceed eight hours so long as the total working hours in the week do not exceed forty-eight. (3) where persons are employed in shifts the eight-hours day and the forty-eight hours week may be exceeded piovided they do not exceed the average of eight hours a day and forty-eight hours a week for a three weeks period.
Mr. BUREAU; In the other case the eight-hour day would be more properly defined as a forty-eight-hour week?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what the Conference decided. It is an eight-hour day and a forty-eight-hour week. In fact that was one of the points of difference in the Conference. The employers wanted the forty-eight-hour week without the eight-hour limitations.
That would be more sen* sible.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-and the employees
wished the straight eight-hour day. If this had been granted in all employments where the Saturday half holiday prevails, it would mean a forty-four-hour week. This Convention was agreed upon as a result of a long conference between employers and employees and representatives of the Government as a fair solution of the differences.

What has the League of Nations to do with this resolution? It stands by itself as I understand it and this Parliament can adopt it or not irrespective of the League of Natidns. Are we not discussing what is on the Order Paper, free from any interference, or control, or request by the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Entirely so. But as there will be before the Government of Canada a proposal dealing with this matter in the form of this Convention when it reaches the Government, I was simply explaining to the House the nature of the Convention so that the House will be seized of the matter and as a good and sufficient reason why this resolution should not be pressed at the present time. Some hon. members, including the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution, asked that the terms of this Convention might be stated for the information of members generally. I have now given the general terms of the Convention and I do not think there is anything to be gained by discussing the details of it at the present time. I will simply mention the further exceptions to the general limitation of hours of work contained in the Convention, because they are important.
Are we going to receive an explanation from the Minister of Justice before this sitting closes?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, the Minister of Justice will give an explanation.
There are exceptions in the case of accidents, actual or threatened also with respect to the processes required in an industry which by nature of the industry must be continuous. Provision is also made for seasonal occupations. So that great elasticity is possible to meet the varying conditions of industry.
Special provision is made for Japan and India and China. Japan makes the greatest advance of any country under the provisions -of this Convention. The only law of Japan at the present time limiting hours of work is the one regulating the horns of work for women and I think that is twelve or thirteen hours a day. Japan has no rest day on Sunday but has two holidays in the year. Under this Convention Japan agrees to a limitation in general industries to nine and a half hours a day and in the silk industry to ten hours, and to one rest day a week. In this respect it marks the greatest advance in limiting the hours of labour in any country in the world. That means a great deal for Canada and the United States. In the days that lie before

us the competition, the keenest competition, both as to employers and employees, will come from the great labouring classes in the Orient. It will be a great thing for the people of this continent if by means of a Convention like the present we get the hours of labour in Japan cut down from twelve or thirteen without any rest day each week to nine and a half or ten with a rest day each week, with the expectation that within a few years Japan will come into harmony with the general terms of this Conference. If nothing else were accomplished by the Conference at Washington than bringing Japan up to that point of cooperation with the other industrial nations in regulating the hours of labour, it would be well worth while anc! a great success.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am very happy indeed to meet what seems to be the general desire for an expression of opinion on my part upon the [DOT]question of the constitutional power of this Parliament to deal with the subject matter of this resolution, which, I think is the question that properly arises in connection with it. I quite understand that the natural desire of members for information with regard to the Labour Conference should have led to the very interesting discussion that we have heard on that subject; but I quite agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) that it is in reality-and I think in giving the explanation which he did give the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) recognizes the fact-beside this question.
, The Motion that we have before us is a Motion to this effect:
That it is desirable that to the extent of the jurisdiction of this Parliament a national eight-hour working day should be established immediately, subject only to the right of express private contract.
Now, as was pointed out, if my memory serves me correctly, by the leader of the Opposition, this motion or declaration that such an enactment should be adopted would not meet, and does not meet, the desire of those who want to have an eight-hour day made an obligatory day by law, because this resolution especially provides for an exemption from any rule that may be made wherever by private contract it is stipulated there shall be an exemption; and I understood the hon. member (Mr. Burnham) who moved the resolution to have declared that his resolution, if adopted and action taken upon it, would carry us no further than to establish a state of the law

under which there would be a presumption that a day's work was eight hours.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all. That presumption would be subject to become inapplicable or to be rebutted by any express stipulation in the contract. I think I am correct in that.
Yes, that is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Now, taking that position, I think there is room for little if any doubt-I think I may say for myself that I have no doubt, because one always looks upon a legal question recognizing the fact of the possibility of the existence of other people's opinions-that such a resolution, or an enactment based upon that resolution if adopted would be an enactment dealing with a subject matter entirely outside of the jurisdiction of this Parliament of Canada. Because, after all, what is it that that enactment would be? It would be a presumption applicable in every contract of lease or hire of work. Now the determination and the interpretation of contracts -the presumption that arises in, connection with contracts generally; I will not make exception of any special conditions such as those that appear in Bills that come before Parliament-falls under the designation of " property and civil rights," and to me it seems quite clear that we have no jurisdiction to declare that it shall be a presumption in every contract of lease or hire, where a day is mentioned and no number of hours, that a day means eight hours. I think that is clearly legislation dealing with the interpretation of contracts having to do with property and civil rights within the different provinces, and-giving my opinion, of course, for what it is worth'and for nothing more-I am of opinion that we would have no jurisdiction to enact legislation of that kind.
I would like to point out that of course the opinion of the Minister of Justice is of no binding effect upon this Parliament. It stands as worth what his opinion as a lawyer may be worth, and it has the weight of whatever may be his reputation as a competent lawyer. The Minister of Justice is not charged with advising the House of Commons, still less with imposing upon it his views of the law; he is the adviser of Government and of the departments of Government.
I think I might leave the matter there so far as the constitutional question is concerned as arising in connection with this
resolution. However, I may point out what would be the powers of this Parliament to legislate with regard to the conditions of contracts of lease and hire if by some treaty validly entered into either Canada or any of its provinces became bound to enact some particular legislation upon the subject. If such a condition arose, then under Article 132 of the British North America Act this Parliament iwould have power to legislate for the purpose of giving effect to any obligation imposed either upon the Dominion or upon any of the provinces. It is only from the point of view of the application of that article that we may be led-in fact,
I think we will be necessarily led-to a consideration of the question: Whether anything may arise out of any treaty or any convention that may be submitted to us by the Labour Conference which would confer jurisdiction upon this Parliament to enact such legislation as might be requisite to comply with or carry out the convention.

Might I ask the minister a question? Does he say that this Parliament, in view of section 93 of the British North America Act, giving the power to the province to legislate with regard to property and civil rights, would have any right to entertain jurisdiction until the provinces had or, had not acted with regard to something which should be done in the treaty with foreign nations under section 132?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that raises, not a question of the power of this Parliament, but the question of what would be proper in the action of this Government. If legislation were essential to the carrying out of an obligation imposed upon a province by a treaty made by the British Empire, there would be power in this Parliament to enact that legislation. If the legislation were of a kind which, under the rules of the constitution ^irrespective of any treaty obligation, would fall within the legislative competence of the provincial legislatures, I myself would think it highly proper for the Dominion Government, before it proceeded to enact the legislation required, to ascertain whether the provinces in the exercise of their ordinary jurisdiction were prepared to act. But as an abstract question of law I do not think that the power of this Parliament to act under those circumstances would depend upon previous application to the provinces; the power seems to be given in express terms without any exception or limitation. In regard to that, as of course in regard to everything else, I am giving merely my own opinion, and upon this very question I shall guard myself by saying'

that it is really an offhand opinion, the question only having been brought to my attention this moment.
We would act through the provincial legislature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to give any more off-hand opinions than are necessary, but the words go very far to confer a power to do that which is necessary so that the obligation is carried out, and I would be disposed to think we would be entitled to do something more than pass a law to carry out the obligation,-that being entitled to pass that law we would be entitled to enforce it. I have not the slightest doubt that if it were a matter about property and civil rights in the provinces, and Canada or the provinces became bound by a treaty to enact that kind of legislation, when we enacted it the courts would have to enforce that just the same as though it were a provincial law.
Does the minister take due notice of the fact that the resolution says, " It is desirable?" Would he mind discussing that word " desirable?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a pretty long cry from what is constitutional to what is desirable. I am not suggesting that this Parliament can pass this pious aspiration perhaps that such a law is desirable; but as I understand the resolution it would be in effect a declaration by us that it is desirable to the extent that it is within our constitutional power to enact the legislation; which in my opinion it is not.
Now, do not forget that the hon. gentleman pointed out the other evening that there are parts of this Dominion where we would have constitutional power. In fact, I think someone suggested that the only work done in those parts was by the wolves. However that may be, it does not seem to me that we could declare a national eight-hour day applicable in what remains of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The purpose of the resolution, no doubt, is to declare a national eight-hour day, and I think we might leave out of consideration what possibility there might be of declaring such a day to be effective in those territories. Certainly it would not be a national eight-hour day if put into effect in that way. Opinions, of course, differ on the question whether it is desirable that there should be legislation creating this presumption. That, however, has been threshed out from different points of view, and I do not think that I could add anything of value.

Now, I do not purpose to go into the question of the interpretation of the provisions of the Peace Treaty with regard to the manner in which conventions are to be dealt with by the different powers. I may, however, point out that as I read the provisions of the Treaty-I say this subject, perhaps, to further consideration, though I have very little doubt about it-they do not impose upon the nations an obligation to enact into law the particular conventions adopted. The obligation 's set forth is that the respective governments or the respective countries will bring before the competent authorities a convention for the enactment of legislation or other action. It goes no further than that. The convention goes on to point out that if that competent authority does not adopt legislation or does not act, there is no further obligation upon the country. If that competent authority does adopt legislation or take other action giving effect to the convention then it becomes the duty of the country concerned to report that ratification to the body in authority. When the conventions arrive at their official condition I do not think that we shall be in any very great difficulty in determining what action is incumbent upon us; certainly to the extent that action is incumbent upon us it will be our duty to take it. As I have pointed out, any action incumbent upon us deals in express terms with our bringing the matter before the competent authority.
That would be before the legislatures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. I should say
that unless there can be found in the terms of the Treaty as applied to the convention the creation of an obligation to enact some specific legislation, we shall not 'find what in my opinion are the essential conditions to giving jurisdiction to this Parliament to legislate upon the subject. Upon this question of legislative jurisdiction I understand that very strong opinions adverse to that which I have expressed are entertained by those who speak for some, at all events, of the provinces. In that condition of affairs it may become necessary to have this question authoritatively passed upon. It would be an undesirable situation, if it did arise, that we should fail entirely of action simply because all the different authorities considered that they were not competent to deal with the matter.
Will this Government now try to find out about the jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I might venture to
say that we think we know about the jurisdiction. But if there should arise such a situation as I have been pointing out; if each authority should say:	We have not
the jurisdiction,-then it might become desirable that we should get an authoritative decision as to where the jurisdiction lies. It is not in the power of this Government to impose its view upon the provincial governments, and of course it is not in their power to impose their views upon us. While I am not saying that it will necessarily be done, the House will see that it is readily conceivable that that will become, if not a necessary, at all events a very desirable step to take.

Having regard to the
phraseology of section 132 of the British North America Act, is the minister of the opinion that under this particular Convention there is any obligation resting upon a province as such, irrespective of its being a component part of the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Whether there is an
obligation resting upon a province as such must depend upon what are the obligations in the Treaty. I have difficulty in conceiving that we would make a treaty imposing an obligation upon a province by name. But if by a treaty we undertook an obligation which in the ordinary operation of things could be carried out only by a province, then there would arise an obligation incumbent on that province as the result of the treaty. I do not conceive that the case that is contemplated is the making of a treaty whereby Canada would say: The province of Ontario will do such-and-such a thing. But if Canada undertook to do something which had to be done in the province of Ontario and which, leaving treaty obligations entirely aside, would be a matter to be dealt with by the province, then I think you would have the case that is contemplated in the statute of an obligation incumbent upon a province. I cannot at the moment quite conceive of a situation where you would have a treaty which would in terms undertake that a particular province would do a particular thing. It would be a treaty-making power that would undertake to do it; but in order to make that effective you must have something that is to be done by a province, or at all events through the exercise of powers which ordinarily belong to a province.
Even though this Parliament would over-rule the exclusive jurisdiction of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the case came under Article 132, Parliament, as I understand it, certainly would be entitled to over-rule the exclusive jurisdiction.

You would have to
amend the British North America Act, would you not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, because Article 132 says that.
Tn the terms of Article 132?
Is not the province supreme?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are not in committee. The Minister of Justice has the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where there is concurrent power in the legislature of a province and in the Parliament of Canada to legislate upon the same subject, then the legislation by the Parliament of Canada supersedes the provincial legislation. Even if you treat Article 132 as leaving co-existent with Parliament's competency under Article 132 the competency of the provincial legislatures under section 91, then you have the case of concurrent jurisdiction, and I think that lawyers generally would agree that in such a case the legislation of Parliament would over-ride that of the provinces. But the only purpose of this express provision of Article 132 is to give to Parliament a power which it would have under the general provisions of section 91; by its express terms it confers a power with regard to matters constituting obligation on the part of the province. Therefore I do not think there is any difficulty in the way of its operating to confer-upon Parliament the power to do things which, under other circumstances, would be within the exclusive power of a provincial legislature.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Am I right in gathering from the minister's remarks that as a matter of jurisdiction this Parliament has no power to enact what is called the eight-hour day?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to say that there is no possible combination of circumstances-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I mean, generally speaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand the enactment of an eight-hour day to mean the enactment of a general law that in all contracts for the lease or hire of labour the day shall be eight hours and no more.

Eliminating all questions of carrying out Treaty obligations, my own opinion would be that Parliament has not the power to enact that legislation.
Unless Parliament made it a criminal offence to work longer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. If Parliament felt justified, I suppose it is within its power to take matters which in their very nature one disassociates entirely from the idea of crime, and by declaring certain things with regard to them to he crimes, to put the matter into our jurisdiction in that way. But I myself would not be disposed to do that.

Very few
would.
Mr. JOHN H. BURNHAM (West Peterborough) : Mr. Speaker, some days ago it was pointed out in the newspapers that the Drury Government in Ontario did not intend to put the eight-hour day upon their legislative programme, but intended to hand the matter over to a commission to find out what it might find out. It naturally occurred to me that it would also be advisable for us in this House to find out, if we did not know, and at any rate to declare our position with regard to the eight-hour day in order that the province of Ontario and all the other provinces might know what the scope of their jurisdiction was with regard to it. We have tonight received f,om the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) the explicit declaration that in his opinion-that is, such an opinion as he would give in advising the Government -this Parliament has no jurisdiction to consider a national eight-hour working day. That liberates, in my opinion, the province of Ontario and enables them to go on promptly with the work of enacting an eight-hour working day if they wish.
All this talk about whether or not the farmer w'ould stand for it, has nothing whatever to do with the question. It was all very interesting, although I knew it all before personally. As to the point: Is the eight-hour day desirable?-strange to say, among all the mighty legal minds in this House not one of them has fastened upon the essential word in the introduction of the resolution. [DOT] A resolution, as I understand it, is to enable the House to give an academic opinion after an academic discussion. But this House refused to consider the question whether an eight-hour day was desirable or not, and that is all I 
wanted them to consider. If they said it was desirable, then the next step was to be taken. If they said it was not desirable, that would have finished it. But they did not, and would not, consider whether or not it was desirable. They simply attacked, almost every one of them, the principle of the eight-hour day.
The object of the resolution has been fully attained, and as it serves no further purpose than that declared by the Minister of Justice I beg leave to withdraw the resolution, Mr. Speaker.
Motion withdrawn.
On motion of Sir George Foster, the House adjourned at 10.35 p.m.
Tuesday, March 16, 1920.
